republic-of-lakotah.story:
The Republic of Lakotah was a proposed independent country for the Lakota, a Native American people often grouped under the name Sioux. Its claimed land covered about 200,000 square kilometres of the northern Great Plains in the United States, in parts of North Dakota, South Dakota, Nebraska, Wyoming and Montana. That land now holds Indian reservations and non-Native towns alike.

The background is a set of treaties. In the 1800s the United States signed treaties with the Lakota as it would with a foreign power, and the 1851 Treaty of Fort Laramie set out a large Lakota territory. The proposed borders copied that treaty: the Yellowstone River to the north, the North Platte to the south, the Missouri to the east and an irregular line to the west. A later dispute is central to Lakota grievances. The United States took the Black Hills of South Dakota for gold mining after the collapse of the 1868 Fort Laramie treaty. In 1980, in United States v. Sioux Nation of Indians, the Supreme Court awarded eight Sioux tribes $105 million as compensation but gave back no land. The tribal governments have refused the money.

On 17 December 2007 four activists calling themselves the Lakota Freedom Delegation went to Washington, D.C., and contacted the State Department. Their leader was Russell Means, a prominent member of the American Indian Movement since the late 1960s, who called himself chief facilitator of a provisional government. The others were Garry Rowland, Duane Martin and Phyllis Young. Their statement said the Lakota were withdrawing from the treaties, citing the colonial apartheid of the reservation system, along with unemployment, poverty, disease and repeated treaty violations. It invited the United States to negotiate and warned that otherwise Lakotah would file liens, which are legal claims against property, on real estate deals across the five states.

The plan on paper was a loose confederation. Citizenship would be open to any resident of any race, with its own passports and driving licences, no nationwide taxes, and local taxes only with the consent of those taxed. The provisional capital was to be Porcupine, South Dakota. In January 2008 the group suggested that independence could follow a Compact of Free Association, the arrangement the United States has with Palau, Micronesia and the Marshall Islands.

The main weakness was support among the Lakota themselves. The delegation dismissed the elected tribal governments as "stay-by-the-fort Indians", and those governments had not been consulted. The Rosebud Sioux and Cheyenne River chairmen said publicly that they did not back it. A treaty has two sides, and one side can announce that it is leaving, but the other side does not have to answer. The State Department referred questions elsewhere, and a Bureau of Indian Affairs official said the withdrawal did not mean anything.

In 2008 the group filed liens on federal land in a South Dakota county, and these were rejected. It asked embassies for recognition without success. Means ran for president of the Pine Ridge Reservation that year, treating the vote as a test of support, and lost 2,277 to 1,918. Nothing significant is reported after that, and the case was never tested in a court. The claim rested on real treaties with a named people, and it still lacked backing from the Lakota's own governments and any response from the United States.

republic-of-madawaska.story:
The Republic of Madawaska was a self-declared state on the Saint John River, in the corner of North America where Maine in the United States now meets New Brunswick and Quebec in Canada. It existed for about three months in 1827, and its flag still flies in Edmundston, New Brunswick.

It arose from a badly drawn border. The 1783 Treaty of Paris, which ended the American Revolution, described the line between the United States and British North America imprecisely, so both sides claimed the same forest and river land for almost 60 years. The Madawaska settlement, mostly French-speaking, had 2,487 people in 1830, while hardly anyone else lived in the area.

John Baker, an American settler, arrived in 1817 and lived where Baker Brook, named after him, meets the Saint John. He was convinced the land belonged to Maine and in 1825 asked the state to take the settlement in. In 1827 he began defying British authority directly. He tried to stop mail being carried by canoe to Quebec, urged French residents to reject British rule, and blocked a constable from making an arrest.

On 4 July 1827 he held an Independence Day party at his house, invited all the settlers, of whom 16 families were American, and raised a flag sewn by his wife, Sophronia Rice. He said the territory was free of all foreign rule and answerable only to the United States. He then drew up the Madawaska Compact, under which signers would settle disputes through elected arbiters and stay away from British officials. Baker would lead as General with two other men, and after a year the republic would ask Maine to annex it. So the republic was intended as a stepping stone to joining a state, and its founders did not plan to stay independent.

On 10 August a local magistrate arrived to confiscate the paper and told Baker to submit. Baker refused and travelled to Portland to ask how far Maine would protect him. He returned to find a warrant out, and on 25 September he was arrested before dawn. He spent 13 months in jail in Fredericton, and in May 1828 a jury convicted him of opposing British authority and fined him £25.

The border dispute went on until the Webster-Ashburton Treaty of 1842, a deal between Britain and the United States that split the Madawaska communities between New Brunswick, Maine and Quebec. The republic never ran as a working government. It shows how an unsettled border invites such a declaration, and how two states can then settle the question between themselves.

republic-of-molossia.story:
Molossia is 11.3 acres of private land near Dayton, Nevada, in the United States, whose owner Kevin Baugh runs it as a joke country and calls himself President. It is a micronation, which means a small self-declared country that no real government recognises. Its president shows visitors around in a sash and sunglasses.

The idea began in 1977, when Baugh and his friend James Speilman, teenagers in Portland, Oregon, watched the film The Mouse That Roared, about a tiny country that attacks the United States. They set up the Grand Republic of Vuldstein, with James as king and Baugh as prime minister. James lost interest, and the country travelled with Baugh through his US Army career under other names, including the Kingdom of Zaria. It took its present name and location after he bought the Nevada land in 1998. He later worked in human resources for the Nevada National Guard, and treating the project as play kept it from causing him trouble in that job.

A visit runs like a small theatre piece. A customs booth asks for pocket change in a tin can. A sign lists banned items, among them catfish, spinach, onions, walruses, missionaries and salesmen. The tour takes in a miniature railroad, national parks and a space programme that consists of a stomp rocket. Baugh stamps passports and hands out money made of paper circles on poker chips. The currency is the Valora, set at 80 American cents, and the law sets a 500 Valora fine for setting off a nuclear device. Molossia says it has been at war with East Germany since 1983, because army drills there cost Baugh his sleep, and argues that the war continues because an island Cuba gave to East Germany was left out of the treaties ending the Cold War.

The Independent reported 27 citizens. No member of the United Nations recognises it. Its relations with the real state are simple. Baugh pays property tax to Storey County and calls the payments foreign aid, so the county has no dispute with him. Baugh describes the project as an expression of personal sovereignty, creativity and political satire. Land stays under county, state and federal law when its owner gives it a new name, and Molossia gives those governments no reason to act, because the tax is paid and nothing is demanded of them.

republic-of-montmartre.story:
The Republic of Montmartre is a charitable association of artists in the Montmartre district of Paris, France, run in the style of a mock republic. Montmartre is the hilltop neighbourhood long associated with painters and cabarets. The association was created in 1921, after the First World War, to protect the character of the district from property developers and to keep alive the artists' habit of helping one another. The City of Paris credits the illustrator Joe Bridge with proposing it on 7 May 1921, while a list of micronations names the cartoonist Jean Barrez.

It has a president, ministers, ambassadors and more than 500 volunteer members, who wear a red scarf, black cape and black hat. Its motto means doing good with joy. The republic's work is ordinary charity. It holds Christmas celebrations for local children, gives money to groups that work with disadvantaged children, and runs exhibitions, book fairs and concerts. It remains active today.

It has no separate status in French law. The form of a state is used here for fun and fundraising, with no claim against France. Its offices and ministers are titles within an association.

republic-of-saugeais.story:
Le Saugeais is a wooded valley in the Haut-Doubs in eastern France, along the Swiss border, that has called itself a republic since a lunchtime joke in 1947. It covers 11 villages, with Montbenoît as its capital. Its sense of being a separate place is old. Canons from a Swiss abbey were given the valley in the Middle Ages, cleared the forest with settlers from Savoy and elsewhere, and ruled the land from the abbey at Montbenoît until the French Revolution. A code of local rules dates from 1458, and the settlers' dialect, called Sauget, was still commonly spoken around 1900.

In 1947 Louis Ottaviani, the prefect of the Doubs, meaning the senior government official for the region, stopped to eat at the Hôtel de l'Abbaye in Montbenoît. The owner, Georges Pourchet, jokingly asked whether he had a permit to enter the Republic of Saugeais. Ottaviani played along. A republic needs a president, he said, and he appointed Pourchet. An official's joke had no legal force, but Pourchet took up the title.

Pourchet died in 1968, and the post stayed empty for four years. Meanwhile the parish priest, Martial Jeantet, found money to restore the abbey, and interest in local folklore grew. In 1972 Pourchet's widow Gabrielle organised a dinner to raise money for the abbey and was made president for life. She gave the joke a structure, appointing a prime minister, a secretary-general, 12 ambassadors and more than 300 honorary citizens, and creating coins and a passport. A song written in the dialect in 1910 became the anthem. A flag based on the old colours of Franche-Comté followed in 1981. In 1987 the French postal service, a real state body, issued a stamp showing the republic's symbols, and a banknote came out in 1997.

Georgette Bertin-Pourchet, Gabrielle's daughter, later became president by unanimous vote, and on 18 March 2022, aged 88, she handed the post to her prime minister, Simon Marguet. The government also has two customs officers. France does not recognise the republic, and no challenge from the state is reported. French institutions have joined in the fun, which shows how little the title changes.

republic-of-texas-group.story:
The Republic of Texas is the name used by several linked groups in the American state of Texas which say the state's 1845 annexation by the United States was illegal, and that Texas is still an independent nation under occupation. Some have been described as militias. Texas really was an independent country for about nine years before joining the United States, which gives the idea its appeal.

Richard Lance McLaren started the movement and claimed to have restored a provisional government on 13 December 1995. He pointed to the 1861 vote in which Texans chose four to one to leave the Union at the start of the Civil War, leaving out the violence and threats used to keep Union supporters from voting. He then argued that Texas had been a captive nation of war since 1865 under international law, a claim scholars do not support. Activists claim more than 40,000 supporters. Money came from donations and from selling items such as Republic of Texas passports. The groups also set up their own courts and sent official-looking papers to real judges and officials.

The movement split into three factions in 1996. In 1997 McLaren and his followers, based in the Davis Mountains of west Texas, kidnapped Joe and Margaret Ann Rowe, held them at the Davis Mountain Resort and demanded the release of a member in exchange. A week-long standoff with police and Texas Rangers followed, until McLaren's wife Evelyn convinced him to give up. He and four others went to prison, and his projected release date is 2041. Two members slipped away. Rangers shot Mike Matson dead two days later, and Richard Keyes III surrendered that September and was sentenced in June 1998 to 90 years. Two members of another faction were convicted in 1998 of threatening to assassinate officials including President Bill Clinton, and each got 24 years.

The legal theory lost separately. On 30 April 1998, in a case brought by the McLarens, a federal district court in the District of Columbia wrote that Texas became the 28th state in 1845 and that "The Republic of Texas no longer exists." The same theory failed in 2004 when a man jailed in Aspen, Colorado, argued that his town had once been part of the old republic and that Colorado therefore could not send him to California.

What remained of the movement joined under an interim government in 2003, based in Overton, Texas, whose headquarters burned down in 2005. In February 2015 the FBI and state and local officers raided a meeting of about sixty followers in Bryan, Texas, because a member had issued fake writs and a fake subpoena ordering a real judge and a lawyer to attend the group's hearings. They seized computers and phones and made no arrests.

For someone founding a territory, the sequence matters. A court can reject the historical argument in a few lines. Police act when the claim turns into hostage-taking, threats or forged court papers, and those cases are decided under ordinary criminal law.

republic-of-uzupis.story:
Užupis is a neighbourhood of less than one square kilometre in Vilnius, the capital of Lithuania, that artists declared an independent republic as a local celebration. Its name means beyond the river, because it lies on the far side of the Vilnele river, and a bridge marks the way in. Around 7,000 people live there, about 1,000 of them artists. Under Soviet rule the district was derelict and dangerous. One main road was called the Street of Death, for its crime and for the Jewish population destroyed in the Holocaust.

When the Soviet Union fell in the early 1990s, many plinths across Vilnius stood empty after their statues were removed. In 1995 local artists used one for a statue of the American musician Frank Zappa, who had never been there, as a symbol of freedom. Two years later, on 1 April 1997, April Fools' Day, they went further and declared the district independent. A founder, Tomas Čepaitis, later cited the old idea that a good country should have no more than about 5,000 citizens, small enough that everyone knows everyone and cheating is hard.

The republic has a president, Romas Lileikis, a government with foreign and tourism ministers, its own unofficial currency, and a navy of three or four small boats used for ceremonies. An army of about 10 men has been retired. Its flag shows a blue hand with a hole in the palm, unable to hold a bribe. The border goes unguarded except on Užupis Day, 1 April, when visitors can have their passports stamped on the bridge.

Lileikis and Čepaitis wrote the constitution in about three hours one afternoon in 1998, after Lileikis came round to take a bath because he had no hot water. That is why its 41 clauses include a right to hot water, heating in winter and a tiled roof, along with lines such as "a dog has a right to be a dog". The text is displayed on mirrored plates along a road called the Avenue of Constitutions, in more than 30 languages.

Foreign governments do not recognise Užupis, and no dispute with the Lithuanian state is reported. Residents remain Lithuanian citizens under Lithuanian law, and the republic has become a source of pride in Vilnius. The state can treat it as local culture at no cost, because the claim takes nothing from the state's law or taxes.

republic-of-vevcani.story:
Vevčani is a village of about 2,400 people near Lake Ohrid in North Macedonia, in the Jablanica Mountains along the border with Albania, that has tried independence more than once. Its isolated terrain let it keep its own habits under the Ottoman Empire and communist Yugoslavia, including its Orthodox religion, a Slavic dialect found nowhere else, and a January carnival said to be 1,400 years old.

The first clash was over water. The Vevčani springs are at the centre of the village's celebrations. In May 1987 the Yugoslav government planned to divert the spring water to new villas by Lake Ohrid for the communist elite. Villagers spent the summer building barricades and threatening to secede. Special police with batons were sent in during what became known as the Vevčani Emergency, which lasted three months, and the government then backed down. Protests over the arrests and injuries continued on and off in Skopje and Belgrade for four years.

When Yugoslavia broke up, the republics that made up the federation each held referendums. Macedonia declared independence on 8 September 1991. On 19 September the village declared itself an independent republic as well, with only 36 of about 2,000 voters against. Macedonia never recognised this, but its government was also dealing with armed separatists in ethnic Albanian areas and was prepared to make a local concession. In 1994 it let Vevčani separate from the larger Struga municipality and form its own municipality, which still exists. So the bid won a legal result, in the form of ordinary local government inside the new state.

In 2002 locals revived the republic as a light-hearted way to draw tourists and poke fun at politics. They fly a flag beside the national one at the municipal building, and they sell red passports with dated entry stamps at souvenir stands, along with their own printed money. North Macedonia governs the village as part of its territory. The real gain from the secession came from the 1994 municipal status, while the passports and banknotes that came later bring in tourists and have no legal effect.

rough-and-ready.story:
Rough and Ready is a small community in the Sierra Nevada foothills of Nevada County, California, in the United States, about 100 kilometres from Sacramento, which declared itself a separate country for less than three months in 1850. It began in the California Gold Rush, when thousands of people came west to dig for gold. In fall 1849 a mining company from Wisconsin settled there, led by Captain A. A. Townsend, who had served under General Zachary Taylor. Taylor's nickname was Old Rough and Ready, and he had just become president, so the company and the camp took the name.

On 7 April 1850 the town declared secession from the Union as the Great Republic of Rough and Ready, largely to avoid taxes on mining. Residents voted to rejoin on 4 July that year. Because they gave up the claim themselves, no government had to put it down and no court ever ruled on it. How the republic was run in those weeks is not known.

A post office arrived by February 1851. The town still celebrates the republic each year for tourism and local pride, and it is a California Historical Landmark. It had 905 people in the 2020 census.

ruterberg.story:
Rüterberg is a village on the Elbe River in northern Germany that declared itself a republic the day before the Berlin Wall fell. From 1949 Germany was split in two. The village lay in communist East Germany, on the stretch of the Elbe that formed the border with West Germany. By the end of the communist period a wall surrounded it, cutting it off from the rest of East Germany as well as from the West.

From 1988 local residents, led by Hans Rasenberger, discussed creating a free town with the power to make its own laws, breaking its ties with East Germany. An assembly of 90 citizens proclaimed the republic on 8 November 1989. The Berlin Wall fell on 9 November, and within a year East Germany itself had ceased to exist, so the state the villagers had opposed was gone before it could respond.

The village became part of reunified Germany. On 14 July 1991 the secretary of state of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, the German state it now sits in, acknowledged the people's right to use the title Dorfrepublik, or Village Republic. The title is an honour, and it gives the village no separate power. Rüterberg is now a district of the town of Dömitz, under ordinary German local government.

shanhaiwoo.mechanism: A temporary gathering of visitors stays under the law of the host country and makes no claim on its territory, so it needs only hotel rooms and visas.
shanhaiwoo.story:
ShanhaiWoo, written 山海坞 in Chinese, is a series of pop-up cities, meaning temporary communities that gather in one place for a limited time and call themselves a city. People who work on cryptocurrency and related technology come together for weeks, live near one another and build projects. A list of such gatherings by the newsletter Agartha places it in China and Thailand, and a report by IOSG counts it among the communities that met in Chiang Mai, Thailand, in October 2024.

Its Singapore edition gives the clearest picture of how it runs. It was a one-month village in September 2025 open to 200 builders by application, covering Ethereum, artificial intelligence and related technology. Early teams valued under $30 million could apply. Participants chose their own hotels, with discounts offered, and the programme began with a town hall meeting and an opening ceremony on 5 September. Backers named on the event page include DRK Lab, AltLayer, Blockchain Builders Fund and HashKey Capital, and scholarships paid for some students.

No individual founders are named, and attendance at earlier editions is not known. Its participants are visitors, who remain under the law of the host country, and it makes no claim on territory. Writers on such gatherings describe them as a possible first step towards permanent communities.

slowjamastan.story:
Slowjamastan is a patch of private desert in Imperial County, California, in the United States, that its owner declared an independent country. The 11.07 acres lie beside State Route 78, about 100 miles from San Diego and 14 miles southwest of the Salton Sea. It has a large border sign, a border post and an open desk that serves as the office of its ruler. Nobody lived there as of February 2025.

Its founder is Randy Williams, a San Diego radio DJ known as R Dub! who presents a show of slow jams, a type of romantic soul music. Williams had visited every United Nations member state but one when he toured Molossia, a joke country in Nevada, in August 2021. He came home wanting one of his own, bought the land that October for $19,000 and declared independence on 1 December 2021. He calls himself sultan and describes the government as a dictatorship with occasional democracy, along with a virtual parliament.

It works largely online. People apply for citizenship and cabinet posts on its website, and more than 25,000 had become citizens by March 2026. It issues passports with quotations from hip hop artists and prints banknotes in a currency called the duble. Its laws come from Williams's everyday annoyances and ban Crocs, mumble rap, and feet on the dashboard. Plans for a bowling alley, armadillo farm and lazy river depend on finding a working water supply. It has appeared at micronation conferences, and Williams attended the 2024 NATO summit in Washington as a guest.

Williams bases his claim on the Montevideo Convention, a 1933 treaty that lists the features of a state as a permanent population, a defined territory, a government and the capacity to deal with other states. Slowjamastan has no permanent population, and no government deals with it as a state. Local business owners have welcomed the attention. Buying land gives the right to use it, while the authority of Imperial County, California and the United States over it continues, so the project stays a form of publicity and entertainment.

snake-hill.story:
The Principality of Snake Hill is a self-declared country near Mudgee in New South Wales, Australia, started by a family in debt. It claims land the size of Monaco and is said to have hundreds of citizens. The Jensen family could no longer afford their taxes and had been in court over a mortgage, which is a loan secured on a home, so that the lender can take the home if the loan is not repaid.

They took their inspiration from the Principality of Hutt River, a Western Australian farm whose owner declared independence in 1970 during a dispute over wheat quotas. The Jensens declared independence on 2 September 2003. In 2006 the project appeared in a Lonely Planet guide to home-made nations. Paul Jensen died in 2010, and his widow Helena took over. That year their daughter Paula spoke at a micronations summit in Sydney.

Independence did not change what they owed. In 2011 the Bank of Queensland foreclosed on, or took back, their home, a property named Castle Hill, which they called their embassy. They tried to block its sale by lodging caveats, legal notices claiming an interest in a property. They also argued that the bank's action lay outside the court's power, because it was a matter of international law for the High Court of Australia or the International Court of Justice. A judge of the New South Wales Supreme Court dismissed these claims in late February 2011.

Paula Jensen appeared often in the state's courts until 2014. No government recognises Snake Hill. The case shows the point at which a claim of sovereignty meets daily life. A bank and a court need only find that a loan exists and has not been repaid, and they have no need to discuss whether the borrower has left Australia.

sovereign-yidindji-government.story:
The Sovereign Yidindji Government is a government set up by members of the Yidindji, an Aboriginal people of northern Queensland in Australia, who renounced their legal ties with Australia in 2014 (a list of micronations says 2013). Aboriginal peoples lived on the continent long before Britain claimed it, and some argue that their sovereignty, the right to rule themselves, was never given up. The Yidindji government is an attempt to act on that argument.

Gudju Gudju Gimuybara is chief minister and Murrumu Walubara Yidindji is foreign and trade minister. The claimed area covers about 2,500 square kilometres south of Port Douglas, through the city of Cairns and inland across the Atherton Tablelands, plus 80 kilometres of sea.

It issues its own driver's licences and number plates. This is where the claim met the state. In May 2015 Queensland police charged Murrumu after finding him with a licence and plates from the Yidindji government, and he argued that the police had no jurisdiction, or legal authority, over him. How the case ended is not known.

In 2022 the group launched a digital Sovereign Yidindji Dollar, pegged to the Australian dollar and said to be backed by gold and silver. It hopes for a memorandum of understanding, a formal written agreement, with the Australian government, and it has approached Russia and Venezuela about diplomatic relations. No such agreement or recognition is known. The case differs from a joke country because its founders belong to a people with a claim that predates the state.

sultanate-of-msimbati.story:
The Sultanate of M'Simbati was a private estate in what is now Tanzania, on the coast of East Africa about 25 kilometres southeast of Mtwara, whose English owner declared it independent. Latham Leslie-Moore was born in London in 1893 and served as an artillery officer in the First World War. He bought the property at auction in the 1940s, when the area was the British colony of Tanganyika.

In 1959 he declared the land separate, named himself sultan, and wrote to the colonial governors asking for recognition, meaning acceptance as a state. He used a flag of red, blue and green with the British Union Flag in the corner. Tanganyika became independent and later joined Zanzibar to form Tanzania, and he wrote to President Julius Nyerere and the United Nations as well. None of them recognised it, and the land stayed part of their territory.

Little is known about how the estate ran. It appeared in John Heminway's 1983 book No Man's Land: The Last of White Africa. A list of micronations gives 1980 as its end, and ruins of its so-called palace remain.

sunda-empire.story:
The Sunda Democratic Empire was an invented empire based in or near Bandung, on the Indonesian island of Java, claiming to succeed the empire of Alexander the Great and to have authority over all countries. It had no link to the Sundanese, the local people of West Java, according to its own spokesman. Its history runs through a money scam, an immigration case and a viral video.

Around 2003 Nasri Banks learned of the empire from unnamed sources, and his wife Raden Ratna Ningrum said it descended from Alexander. That year a man named Jhonson Low showed Nasri a certificate for a deposit of 2 billion dollars at an offshore bank, and the couple gave him money to recover it. Their daughter Fathia later received a paper for 500 million dollars addressed to her as a princess. Believing the story, she and her sister Lamira set off to research the empire.

In July 2007 Malaysia detained the sisters for trying to enter Sarawak from Brunei on Sunda Empire diplomatic passports. A court freed them in January 2008, but they went on claiming Sunda Empire citizenship and refused to accept Indonesian citizenship. That left Malaysia with nowhere to deport them, so the authorities treated them as stateless, meaning belonging to no country, and held them at an immigration depot under the supervision of the UN refugee agency.

The group was active from 2017. In early 2020 a video spread online showing Rangga Sasana, calling himself secretary general, addressing people in military-style uniforms and blue berets. He invited all countries to register with the empire, which he said would settle their debts to the World Bank. Indonesian Wikipedia articles on the United Nations and NATO were altered to mention it. Police arrested the leaders for fraud that January.

At trial in June 2020, Nasri said the declaration was an attempt to have his daughters sent home. Indonesian courts did not need to rule on the history of the empire. All three were sentenced to two years in prison under ordinary law, for spreading false information and disturbing the peace, and they were freed in 2021 under a pandemic release policy. Rangga Sasana became a minor internet personality and died in December 2022. Scholars have worried that such invented kingdoms, which appeared at about the same time elsewhere in Java, could use romantic tales of ancient rulers to deceive people.

telosa.story:
Telosa is a proposed new city in the United States that has not been built. In September 2021 the billionaire Marc Lore, who founded Jet.com and sold it to Walmart, announced a plan for a city on 150,000 acres of cheap desert land, at a stated cost of $400 billion. It would hold 5 million people, by 2050 in some reports and over 40 years in others. A first phase would house 50,000 people on 1,500 acres at over $25 billion, with first residents hoped for by 2030. The name comes from the Greek word telos, meaning purpose.

The unusual part is how it would be paid for. Lore blames many of capitalism's problems on the way land is owned, and he draws on the economist Henry George, who argued that land value should benefit the community. A city raises the value of land simply by existing, and under normal ownership that gain goes to landowners. In Telosa a community endowment, a fund held for all residents, would own the land. People could be licensed to build on it and to sell the structures, while the gain in land value would go to the community.

The design came from the architects Bjarke Ingels Group. It has a 15-minute layout with homes, jobs and schools close together, a ban on fossil-fuel vehicles, and a central tower called Equitism. Funding was to come from private investors, philanthropists, federal and state grants and development subsidies, and planners said they would approach state officials soon.

No site had been chosen, with Nevada, Utah, Arizona, Idaho, Texas and the Appalachian region named as options, and no construction is reported. Telosa does not seek independence. Its founders would need land and approvals from a US state, and it would remain under state and federal law. It proposes a new way of running a community while staying inside a country, which avoids any dispute over sovereignty. The obstacle it has met so far is finding the land and the money.
