vemerana.story:
Vemerana was a breakaway state declared in 1980 on Espiritu Santo, the largest island of the Pacific country of Vanuatu. Until that year Vanuatu was the New Hebrides, governed by Britain and France together under an arrangement called a condominium, with two sets of officials. France and Britain agreed it would become independent on 30 July 1980, and the question was who would control it afterwards.

Nagriamel was a movement founded in 1966 at a meeting of chiefs on Santo. It wanted European-owned land that lay unused returned to islanders, and by 1969 it had about 10,000 members, about one in eight of the population. Jimmy Stevens, who had first come to the chiefs offering to sell them guns, became its leader and built a farm complex at Vanafo. Nagriamel argued that the islands were not ready for independence. It lost to the English-speaking Vanua'aku Pati, led by Walter Lini, and it had the support of French-speaking landowners and anti-independence French interests.

The outside money came from the Phoenix Foundation, an American libertarian group run by Michael Oliver, which had already backed attempts to create new states at Minerva Reef and Abaco. It wanted a tax haven in the islands. Stevens's trial later revealed that he and Nagriamel had received 250,000 American dollars from it.

From June 1980 Stevens's followers blockaded the airport at Santo, destroyed two bridges and declared the State of Vemerana. On 8 June the government asked Britain and France for troops. Both sent them, but France refused to let them act against the rebels, and it was later found to have secretly supported Stevens. Vanuatu became independent on schedule, and Lini, as incoming prime minister, asked Papua New Guinea for help. That country sent troops in its first overseas deployment. The foreign press called it the Coconut War.

The rebels had mainly bows and arrows, rocks and slings, and islanders generally welcomed the soldiers, and there were few casualties. In late August soldiers fired on a vehicle that burst through a roadblock and killed Stevens's son, and on 28 August Stevens surrendered. Reprisals against his supporters spread through the northern islands. He was sentenced to 14 years, was freed in 1991 and died in 1994. Nagriamel went on as an ordinary political party and has won seats in Vanuatu's parliament.

The foreign investors depended on a local movement with a real grievance over land. That movement then had to fight a newly independent government that a neighbouring state was ready to help, and the money from abroad could not change the result.

add_sources.t: Nagriamel (Wikipedia)

set.founder: Christopher Barry Joseph Beyette (King Christopher I), a television news cameraman

vikesland.why: Filled in the founder's name, which the earlier entry lacked, from the Wikipedia article on Vikesland.
vikesland.story:
The Kingdom of Vikesland was a micronation, a self-declared country that no government recognises, in Manitoba, Canada. Christopher Beyette, a television news cameraman for the CHUM network, founded it in 2005 and took the title King Christopher I. He meant its creation to be the subject of a documentary film about micronations.

The project later shifted to unspecified charity work and to contact with other micronations, including the Grand Duchy of Westarctica and attendees of the MicroCon meeting in 2015. Its website said it was not secessionist and did not claim Canadian territory, yet the same site named as Vikeslandic territory his home near Brandon and a rural property of 6.5 square kilometres, the Royal Ranchlands, which he owned with his parents. It changed its flag in 2015.

The kingdom was dissolved in April 2018. A revival as the Jarldom of Vikesland was mentioned for 2019, but nothing further happened and the website had gone by the end of that year. No response from the Canadian government is known, and none was needed, because the project made no demand on the state and ordinary property law continued to apply.

add_sources.t: Kingdom of Vikesland (Wikipedia)

vitalia.story:
Vitalia was a temporary village focused on longevity, the science of living longer, held in February 2024 in Próspera. Próspera is a privately run zone on the Honduran island of Roatán, set up under a Honduran law that allowed such zones their own legal rules. Longevity advocates at the earlier Zuzalu gathering had made a new jurisdiction and rules for longevity science a main topic, and Próspera offered a place with separate rules.

The village had a laboratory for biohacking, meaning self-experiment to improve the body, along with workout groups and a biomedical hackathon, a contest to build projects quickly. It is listed as a spin-off of Zuzalu, an earlier pop-up village in Montenegro. Its organisers hoped it would lead to a permanent home base, and it is not known to have one.

It ended after its 2024 session. Vitalia made no claim of its own to govern land. Its legal footing was borrowed from Próspera, so its standing depended on how Honduras treats that zone. How many people attended, what it cost and what its experiments found are not known.

add_sources.t: Próspera (Wikipedia)
The milieu of Zuzalu (Contemporary Sciences)

whangamomona.story:
Whangamomona is a small settlement in the interior of New Zealand's North Island that declared itself a republic in protest at a change of local boundaries. It lies on State Highway 43, known as the Forgotten World Highway, 65 kilometres north-east of Stratford. Its statistical area covers about 690 square kilometres and had 159 people in the 2023 census.

New Zealand is divided into regions, each with its own council. In local government reforms in 1989 the town was placed in the Manawatu-Wanganui Region, on the grounds that the Whangamomona River flows into the Whanganui River. Residents wanted to be in the Taranaki Region.

On 1 November 1989, at what they called the first Republic Day, they responded by declaring the Republic of Whangamomona. The declaration began as a pointed protest, and the town kept up the event as a yearly celebration with a vote for president. It became a festival that draws visitors from across the North Island, and in 2001 it moved to every two years, held in January for better summer weather.

No formal response from the New Zealand government is reported. The complaint was about which regional council governs the town, and the residents did not reject New Zealand itself. The republic continues as a local festival, and the town stays fully under New Zealand law.

winneconne-sovereign-state.story:
Winneconne is a village of fewer than 2,000 people in northeast Wisconsin, in the United States, at the meeting of two lakes, known locally as a fishing destination. In 1967 it declared itself a separate state for a day after being left off the official map.

The official state highway map for 1967 showed only a blank little circle where the village should be. In those days travellers relied on printed maps, and residents feared losing tourist money. Local leaders wrote to Governor Warren Knowles asking for a correction. He replied that redrafting the maps was not possible and promised that the village would appear in 1968.

Vera Kitchen, president of the Chamber of Commerce, a local business group, turned this into publicity. A national contest called Here's How to Put Winneconne Back on the Map offered a free weekend as a prize, with support from Congressman William Steiger, and drew over 1,000 entries. The winners were Janice Badtke and Kay Klipstine, two Wisconsin natives working as congressional aides in Washington. Their entry proposed that Winneconne secede, declare war on the United States, seize the post office, detain the postmaster as an enemy alien and ask the United Nations for a peace mission.

The village kept the secession and dropped the war. A declaration went to the governor, and on 22 July 1967 residents lowered the state flag and raised a banner showing a skunk, a sheepshead fish, poison ivy and a dodo, with a motto recalling that the village had been left out. Parades, boat races, community breakfasts and a one-day toll bridge followed.

The governor was in on it from the start. He was honorary chair of the contest and chose the winner, and the village sent him instructions for his part. He phoned to express the state's regrets and to promise that the village would be on the 1968 map and on a highway sign, and the call was broadcast over the village's loudspeakers. The secession ended within 24 hours. The story made national news, and the village has held Sovereign State Days nearly every year since. Nobody pressed any legal claim, and the village got what it wanted through publicity.

zad-notre-dame-des-landes.mechanism: A long occupation can stop a state project and win a negotiated right to stay. The price was each project filing its own claim under the law of the same state, while other sites were evicted.
zad-notre-dame-des-landes.story:
The ZAD of Notre-Dame-des-Landes was a long occupation of a mostly farming area of 1,650 hectares near Nantes in western France, set up to stop a planned airport. ZAD stands for zone à défendre, or Zone to Defend, a play on the official planning term for a development zone. People there ran their own daily life for years on land the state had set aside for a project.

The state had planned an airport there since the 1960s, and local farmers and environmental groups opposed it for decades. As residents were told to leave, some refused and became squatters, and activists joined them, building homes and living in the trees. The first occupation was the Rosiers farm in August 2007. In 2012 the prime minister, Jean-Marc Ayrault, a former mayor of Nantes, said the airport would happen.

In October 2012 the state began an eviction called Operation Caesar, with 2,000 police. Occupiers used barricades, human chains and farmers' tractors. After police destroyed 13 cabins and farmhouses, over 40,000 people marched on 17 November and built a new hamlet by hand, with a bar, kitchen, workshops, dormitories, first aid post and pirate radio, guarded by 40 linked tractors. More than 200 support committees formed across France, and the government backed down.

Daily life grew more settled. By 2017 there were around 70 networked sites, with vegetable plots, a bakery using local grain, a brewery, a pirate radio station, a newspaper and herds of cows, goats and sheep. Decisions were made through shared structures and debate among the occupiers.

On 17 January 2018 Prime Minister Edouard Philippe announced that the airport would be dropped and the existing Nantes airport redeveloped, and said the squatters had until spring to leave. The victory split the occupiers. Some wanted to negotiate with the state, and others wanted to stay fully outside it. In April 2018 the state sent in police, and over 10 days they fired 11,000 tear gas canisters and stun grenades. Squatters reported 272 injuries and police 77. The state estimated that 29 projects had been destroyed and 60 to 70 remained.

Philippe halted the operation on 26 April while the occupiers' representatives sought legal recognition for 28 projects. Fifteen were accepted, including a sheep farm making wool and a buckwheat pancake business, and evictions of other sites resumed in May. By 2019 the projects were seeking leases. The occupiers had stopped the airport, after a campaign of about 50 years, and those who stayed did so under permission from the state, through ordinary French land and farm law.

zapatista-territories.story:
The Zapatista autonomous territories are communities in Chiapas, a poor state in southern Mexico near the Guatemalan border, that have governed themselves outside the Mexican state since 1994. Most of the people are Indigenous Maya farmers. Their movement is named after Emiliano Zapata, a hero of the 1910 revolution who fought for peasants' land.

On 1 January 1994, the day the North American Free Trade Agreement took effect, about 3,000 armed members of the Zapatista Army of National Liberation (EZLN) seized towns and cities in the Chiapas highlands. They burned police stations and occupied government buildings, and they issued a declaration of war on a government they called illegitimate. They demanded work, land, housing, food, health care, education, independence, freedom, democracy, justice and peace. They also seized over a million acres from large landowners. A ceasefire came on 12 January, and the fighters withdrew into their own communities and stayed in control there.

Talks with the government produced the San Andrés Accords of 1996 on Indigenous rights. Mexico has never recognised the region's autonomy. The EZLN rejected a later agreement and created 32 autonomous municipalities on its own authority, carrying out its demands without state help, with some money from international groups. This is a different path from secession. The Zapatistas declared no new country. They run their own affairs and carry out their demands without the state.

Day to day, the communities run their own schools, clinics and farming, police themselves, and follow a Women's Revolutionary Law on the rights of women. Until 2003 they were organised around centres called Aguascalientes. These gave way to regional centres called Caracoles, with municipalities run by Councils of Good Government. Under the movement's own rules, military commanders may not hold government posts. Al Jazeera reported from the village of Oventic in 2014 that the Zapatistas governed and policed their own communities across five regions and that relations with the state stayed strained.

In November 2023 Subcomandante Moisés announced that the autonomous municipalities and councils would dissolve, citing cartel violence along the Guatemalan border and accusing the army of failing to stop it. They were replaced by Local Autonomous Governments, grouped in collectives and regional assemblies, a looser structure, and the Caracoles were closed to outsiders. An anthropologist quoted in reports said the movement had become isolated and that young people were leaving for work and schooling.

No state recognises the territories, and they exist through control on the ground. They have lasted more than 30 years without legal status. Armed force and local support made that possible, and cartel violence is now the main pressure on them according to their own statements.

add_sources.t: Zapatista Army of National Liberation (Wikipedia)

zaqistan.story:
Zaqistan is a four-acre patch of desert in northwestern Box Elder County, Utah, in the United States, which its owner calls a country. Zaq Landsberg, a New York resident, bought the land online in about 2005, when it was only numbers on a GPS to him, and he calls himself its president. The site is about 60 miles from the nearest town and 15 miles from a paved road, followed by a two-mile hike off a dirt track. He keeps the exact location private so that people do not get lost looking for it.

Over several visits he has set up a flag, a border gate, a supply bunker and a robot sentry. He also makes official-looking passports, which visitors can have stamped on the way in and out. He says the project works best when the passports circulate in the real world.

Landsberg calls it an art project that tests the limits of land ownership and sovereignty. He has said that his goal is for it to become a real country and that this is impossible, and that he is going through the motions to find out what those words mean. No country recognises it. He pays property tax to the county and calls these payments tributes, to keep relations friendly. Because the tax is paid, the county has no dispute with him. The land stays in Utah under American law.

zuitzerland.story:
Zuitzerland is a temporary village for technologists and researchers, held at Laax, a mountain resort in the Swiss Alps. It grew out of Zuzalu, a two-month gathering in Montenegro in 2023, and out of defensive accelerationism, or d/acc, a movement that wants to speed up technology that protects people from harm, such as cryptography and biotechnology.

Its organisers call it a network state and society sandbox. A network state is an idea from the entrepreneur Balaji Srinivasan for an online community that hopes in time to gain its own land and rules. A sandbox here means a safe place to experiment. The organisers say Switzerland suits this because of its decentralised politics, and they asked how Swiss government could be improved upon for the age of new technology.

A residency ran from 1 to 26 May 2025. Residents lived and worked there and helped set the agenda for the first two weeks. A public summit on 17 to 19 May included among its announced speakers Ethereum co-founder Vitalik Buterin, E. Glen Weyl, Audrey Tang and Amir Taaki, with talks on brain technology, robot demonstrations and a session titled Farewell to Westphalia, a reference to the 1648 peace treaties often credited with creating the modern system of states. Summit visitors had to find their own rooms. The Network State Atlas, a directory of such projects, lists it as active since 2024 and gives about 150 people per event.

The organisers say they are building a permanent hub in Switzerland. Whether that hub exists is not known, and the group is not known to have claimed legal independence. Everyone present stays under Swiss law, and calling the event a network state gives it no separate standing.

zuzalu.story:
Zuzalu was a temporary community of about 200 people at Lustica Bay, a resort on the Adriatic coast of Montenegro. It was conceived by Vitalik Buterin, a co-founder of the Ethereum cryptocurrency network, and ran for about two months from 25 March 2023. It set the model for later pop-up cities, in which people who met online live in one place for weeks or months.

Participants came from crypto, drug companies, politics and universities. They stayed mostly in resort hotels and rented homes, with the five-star Chedi Lustica Bay as the main base. Topics included cryptocurrency, artificial intelligence and the science of longer life, and the longevity group VitaDAO helped organise a three-day science conference. A main theme of that track was finding a new jurisdiction and set of rules for longevity medicine,.

Another topic was the network state, an idea from the former Coinbase executive Balaji Srinivasan in which an online community eventually buys land and seeks its own laws. Srinivasan appeared by video. The news site Decrypt reported that some compared the event to Burning Man for futurists and others to a sleepaway camp for the crypto elite.

Daily life was loosely organised. Talks and seminars were arranged by participants, breakfast was served every day at a local restaurant taken over for the event, and a philosophy group met in the hotel sauna until the management asked it to stop. One group handed out worthless Venezuelan bolivar notes as party invitations, then built an app that used the serial numbers as a test identity system. The writer Jonathan Hillis later called the location too expensive and inconvenient, and said it had produced no longer-term plan for a permanent base.

No land was taken and no new law was reported. Everyone remained under Montenegrin law and went home when the two months were over. Later projects, including Vitalia and Zuitzerland, grew out of it. It tested how a community organises itself and asked nothing of the host country's law.

add_sources.t: Web3 Pop-Up Villages (P2P Foundation)

100-year-starship.story:
The 100 Year Starship is a project to study how people might one day travel to another star. Even the nearest star is over four light-years away, far beyond any spacecraft that exists, so the first problem is how to keep research going for a century when governments and companies plan over a few years. It began in summer 2010 at DARPA, the US defense research agency, under David Neyland, working with Paul Eremenko. The inspiration was a 1956 Robert Heinlein novel in which a foundation funds technology that takes generations to pay off.

DARPA put in $1 million and NASA's Ames research centre in California $100,000. The plan was a one-year study to find a lasting private way of paying for such research, ending with a grant to a new organisation. Ames director Pete Worden announced the project in October 2010 before the government had finished coordinating it, which caused friction. A workshop of 30 invited scientists and writers in January 2011 listed intellectual property, credibility and governance as immediate problems. The first public symposium, in Orlando that year, drew over 700 people.

In 2012 a group led by the Dorothy Jemison Foundation of former astronaut Mae Jemison won a $500,000 grant and took over the name and DARPA's intellectual property, which moved the project from government to private hands. That year Senator Tom Coburn listed it among the 100 most wasteful federal spending projects, citing a session on whether Jesus died for Klingons too. Symposia followed in Houston, in Graz in 2015 and in Nairobi in 2023, which is the last activity reported.

It matters to the question of territory because of the law a starship would carry. The Outer Space Treaty of 1967 says in Article VI that countries are responsible for their private groups in space and must authorise and keep supervising them. So a ship built by a private foundation in the United States would still need a US licence and supervision. No ship has been built, and the project remains a matter of meetings and papers.

add_sources.t: Outer Space Treaty, full text (UN Office for Outer Space Affairs)

breakthrough-starshot.story:
Breakthrough Starshot is a privately funded plan to send tiny uncrewed probes to the nearest stars. Instead of carrying fuel, each probe would be pushed by light from Earth. The investor Yuri Milner announced it in New York on 12 April 2016 with the physicist Stephen Hawking, and Facebook founder Mark Zuckerberg also sat on the board. Pete Worden, who had run NASA's Ames centre, was executive director.

The method was to carry about 1,000 probes of a few grams each, called StarChips, into high orbit on a mothership. Each would have a thin sail up to 4 metres across. A group of lasers on the ground, spread over about a square kilometre with up to 100 gigawatts of combined power, would push on each sail for about 10 minutes. A gigawatt is about the output of a large nuclear plant. The probes would reach 15 to 20 percent of the speed of light and fly past the planet Proxima Centauri b, a little over 4 light-years away, after 20 to 30 years. A message back would take about four more years.

Initial funding was $100 million, and Milner put the final cost at $5 billion to $10 billion, with a first launch around 2036. In September 2025 Scientific American reported that the project was on hold indefinitely, and the physicist Philip Lubin estimated that about $4.5 million of the $100 million had been spent. No formal cancellation has been reported.

Because the probes carry no people, the project raises no question of settlers' rights, and its legal interest lies on the ground. A laser array of that power would stand on land inside some country, so that country's permission would be needed. Under Article VI of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, the country that authorises the launch also becomes responsible for it. Launch approval was never tested, because the project never reached that stage.

add_sources.t: Outer Space Treaty, full text (UN Office for Outer Space Affairs)

icarus-interstellar.why: The Wikipedia page listed as a source now returns no article. The story rests on the entry's data and the Project Hyperion article.
icarus-interstellar.story:
Icarus Interstellar is a volunteer nonprofit, registered in Alaska in February 2011, that studies how to send craft to other stars. It grew from Project Icarus, a five-year study of a fusion-powered starship started in September 2009 by Kelvin Long and Richard Obousy. That study built on Project Daedalus, a design from the 1970s by the British Interplanetary Society, a space advocacy group. Fusion is the reaction that powers the Sun, and no spacecraft has yet used it. The nonprofit's founders included Andreas Tziolas, Pat Galea and Adam Crowl, and its stated mission is to achieve interstellar flight before the year 2100, aiming at stars within 15 light-years or habitable planets within 22.

Its projects included Hyperion, on ships for many generations, and Persephone, which studied ecosystems for a ship 20 kilometres long and 5 kilometres across, housing 50 to 500 people. A Starship Congress in Dallas in August 2013 drew nearly 200 people, and another was scheduled for September 2015 at Drexel University. Its activity after 2015 is not known, and it has built no ship.

Its legal position is simple. A nonprofit registered in the United States would need US authorisation and supervision if it ever launched anything, because Article VI of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty makes each country answerable for its private groups in space. Registering in Alaska gives the group a legal form inside the United States and no separate standing outside it.

add_sources.t: Outer Space Treaty, full text (UN Office for Outer Space Affairs)

ost-article-viii-open-ended.story:
The Outer Space Treaty is the main international agreement on space. It took effect on 10 October 1967 and had 118 member countries as of October 2025. It was written for rockets and moon landings, and it says nothing specific about ships that would travel between stars. Three of its rules would still apply to such a ship, and one of them sets no distance limit.

Article VI makes each country responsible for what its people and companies do in space, and requires it to authorise and keep supervising private activity. Article VII makes the launching country liable for damage the craft causes. Article VIII says that the country whose official list, or registry, includes a spacecraft keeps "jurisdiction and control" over it and "any personnel thereof" while in outer space or on a celestial body. Jurisdiction means the power to make and apply law.

Article VIII sets no distance at which this authority ends. Suppose a ship registered in one country leaves the solar system with a crew and families aboard. Read literally, that country's law travels with the ship for the whole voyage, and a person born aboard would come under its authority. This matters to anyone planning a ship that would take several generations to reach another star, because the children aboard would be subject to a law they never chose and could not vote on.

The treaty gives few answers to the harder questions. It does not say what happens if the registering country ceases to exist, though ownership of old Soviet spacecraft is treated as passing to Russia as the continuing state. It does not say who counts as a citizen after a birth aboard. Article XVI lets a member leave the treaty on one year's notice, so a country could leave its duties behind. A radio message to a ship light-years away would take years to arrive, which makes continuing supervision hard to imagine in practice.

The treaty also calls astronauts envoys of mankind, and tells other countries to help them in an emergency. No court or government agency is known to have applied these articles to a voyage between stars, and no such ship exists. The rule stands as the closest existing answer, and how it would work over such a span is unknown.

add_sources.t: Treaty on Principles Governing the Activities of States in Outer Space, full text (UN Office for Outer Space Affairs)

project-hyperion.story:
Project Hyperion studies generation ships, meaning crewed ships whose voyage to another star would last longer than a human life. People would be born, live and die on board, and only their descendants would arrive. The researcher Andreas Hein started the project in December 2011 from WARR, a student group at the Technical University of Munich in Germany, as part of the Icarus Interstellar program. Its stated aim is to assess whether crewed interstellar flight could be done with current and near-future technology, and it has led to some of the most detailed designs of such ships so far.

The team published a study in the Journal of the British Interplanetary Society in 2012, including an assessment of world ship designs and of the population needed. In 2014 the researcher Cameron Smith used its data to estimate how large a population must be to stay genetically healthy over the trip. Core members later moved to a similar project at the Initiative for Interstellar Studies and presented results at a European Space Agency workshop in 2019.

A design competition opened in 2024, with one report describing a journey of 250 years. Results came in July 2025. First place went to the Italian team Chrysalis, second to WFP Extreme of Poland and third to Systema Stellare Proximum of Malaysia.

Reports on the project do not say how such a ship would be governed or name a destination, and it remains a paper study. The law would still reach it. Under Article VIII of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, the country that registered the ship keeps legal authority over it and its crew, with no end distance stated. Under Article VI that country must also supervise any private group that launches. So a generation ship would leave Earth as some country's legal responsibility, and the children aboard would be bound by rules set before their birth.

l5-society-oneill.story:
The L5 Society was an American group formed to promote large human settlements in space. The name comes from L5, one of the Lagrange points of the Earth-Moon system. L4 and L5 sit on the Moon's orbit, at equal distances from Earth and the Moon, and an object in orbit around them stays there without using fuel. The orbit around L5 is large enough to hold many settlements.

The idea came from Gerard O'Neill, a physics professor at Princeton University. From 1969 he worked out how big a rotating structure could be built in zero gravity, with rotation pressing people against the inner surface to imitate gravity. The answer was tens of miles across. To avoid the cost of lifting everything from Earth, he proposed building from material mined on the Moon or asteroids. To pay for it, he proposed building solar power satellites, which would beam energy to Earth, giving the colonies something to sell. He published "The Colonization of Space" in Physics Today in September 1974.

Keith Henson and Carolyn Meinel of Tucson, Arizona, read it and wrote to him, and in August 1975 they incorporated the society. Its first newsletter carried a letter of support from the presidential contender Morris Udall and said the long-range goal was to disband the society at a mass meeting at L5. O'Neill's book The High Frontier followed in 1977. O'Neill himself took no part in running the group, which started from his mailing list. No hardware was ever built, and critics said transport costs were far too high for individuals to pay.

Its main effect was legal and political. In 1979 the United Nations produced the Moon Treaty, which treats the Moon's resources as the common heritage of all humanity. The society argued that this would stifle the mining its colonies depended on, and that the treaty would allow searches of space facilities without a warrant. It hired the Washington lobbyist and lawyer Leigh Ratiner, who trained activists including Eric Drexler and Chris Peterson to work the halls of Congress. They concentrated on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee. Nobody was lobbying in favour of the treaty, so a small group could make a difference, and the United States never ratified it.

A country that stays out of a treaty is not bound by that treaty's rules, which is why the campaign still matters to anyone arguing for private use of the Moon. The society also used a phone tree and a database of close to 10,000 members in a fight over funding for solar power satellites in 1980 and 1981. In 1987 it merged with the National Space Institute to form the National Space Society, which still operates.

assange-ecuador-embassy.story:
Julian Assange, the Australian co-founder of the leaks website WikiLeaks, lived for nearly seven years inside Ecuador's embassy in London. The embassy is a suite of rooms on part of the ground floor of a block of flats at 3 Hans Crescent, near the Harrods store, in a building that also holds the Colombian embassy and private apartments.

People often think of an embassy as foreign soil, and it is not. The land stays part of the host country. Under the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations, the treaty on how countries treat each other's diplomats, embassy premises are protected, so the host country's officials may not enter without the permission of the head of the mission. That rule gives a person inside protection from arrest for as long as the embassy lets them stay and no longer.

Sweden wanted to question Assange over four alleged sexual offences. After Britain's Supreme Court dismissed his appeal against being sent there, he breached his bail and entered the embassy on 19 June 2012. Ecuador granted him diplomatic asylum on 16 August. Britain did not accept this, so he could not leave. Police notes photographed outside said he was to be arrested under all circumstances if he came out.

Britain suggested it could use a 1987 British law, the Diplomatic and Consular Premises Act, to enter and arrest him after giving notice, then withdrew the suggestion after Ecuador called this a clear breach of international law. Police instead guarded the building, at a reported cost of £6.5 million in the first two years. By the time the guard was lifted in February 2015 the cost had reached £10 million. He spoke to supporters from a low balcony in August 2012, and Ecuador paid a security company for over five years to monitor his visitors, as the Guardian revealed in 2018.

Swedish prosecutors dropped their investigation in May 2017. In April 2019 President Lenín Moreno accused Assange of repeatedly violating the terms of his asylum and ended it, and on 11 April British police, invited in by Ecuador, arrested him. He was held in Belmarsh prison until June 2024. On 26 June 2024, in the Northern Mariana Islands, he pleaded guilty to one US count of conspiring to obtain and publish national defence information. His sentence of five years and two months was counted as already served in Britain, and he was freed that day.

An embassy kept British police out for seven years, but only on terms set by Ecuador's government. When that government withdrew its permission, the protection ended the same day, and Assange had no way to stop it.

fort-st-angelo-order-of-malta.mechanism: A country can give a recognised body limited special status over a building by treaty while keeping ownership and most of its own law. Each privilege is listed one by one, asylum is barred, and either side can end the deal under the treaty's exit clause.
fort-st-angelo-order-of-malta.story:
Fort St Angelo is a fortress at Birgu on Malta's Grand Harbour, part of which is used under a treaty by the Sovereign Military Order of Malta. The Order is a Catholic lay religious order that runs humanitarian work worldwide and traces its history to the Knights Hospitaller of about 1099. It has an unusual position. It has no territory of its own, yet it has diplomatic relations with more than 110 countries and is treated by many as a sovereign body in international law, though some legal scholars dispute that.

The fort explains the name. The knights rebuilt it from the 1530s to the 1560s and used it as their headquarters during the Great Siege of Malta in 1565. They lost the island to Napoleon's forces in 1798. The British garrisoned the fort from 1800 to 1979. After a first agreement in 1991, Malta and the Order signed a new treaty on 5 December 1998, ratified in 2001 under Chapter 429 of Maltese law.

The treaty lists what is given and what is kept. Malta grants a right of use of the upper part of the fort, including the Grand Master's House and the Chapel of St Anne, as a seat for coordinating the Order's humanitarian work. The Order's seat and archives are inviolable, which means officials may not enter or seize them. Its property is immune from search and confiscation, and its vehicles carry diplomatic plates. It pays no customs duty on goods for official use, and Malta must try to keep water and power flowing on the same terms as for embassies. The Order's own tribunals hear employment disputes with its foreign staff.

Malta keeps the rest. The site cannot be sold, and if the Order stops using it, it returns to Malta. The Maltese flag flies beside the Order's. Except where the treaty says otherwise, Maltese courts have full and exclusive authority and Maltese law applies. The Order may not grant asylum there, and it must hand over to Malta anyone wanted for an offence or for deportation or extradition.

The treaty runs for 99 years, and either side may give notice in the 50th or 75th year. The arrangement is in force. For anyone hoping to obtain territory from a state, this shows what a long-established body with diplomatic ties has obtained for one part of one building. It came with no ownership and with an exit date written into the text.

guantanamo-lease.story:
Guantánamo Bay is a US naval base on 117 square kilometres of land and water at the southeastern end of Cuba, held under a lease since 1903. It is the oldest American naval base overseas.

In 1901 the US Congress passed the Platt Amendment, which said Cuba would sell or lease land to the United States for coaling or naval stations, so that ships could refuel. The Cuban constitutional convention resisted at first, then wrote the amendment into the constitution that took effect in 1902. The lease followed in 1903.

The lease splits two ideas that usually go together. Article 3 says Cuba keeps "ultimate sovereignty", meaning the final legal title, while the United States exercises sole jurisdiction, meaning it alone makes and applies law there. The land may be used as a coaling and naval station only. Rent was $2,000 a year in gold until 1934, when the United States changed it to dollars, and since 1974 it has been $4,085 a year. A 1934 treaty says the lease can end only if both sides agree or the United States leaves the base. So the United States can hold on for as long as it chooses, simply by staying.

From 1953 to 1959 thousands of Cubans commuted to jobs on the base. After the revolution, the government that took power in 1959 began protesting that the base had been imposed by force and is illegal under international law. Cuba has cashed only one rent cheque since then, and Fidel Castro said that one was deposited by mistake. In late 1961 Cuban troops planted an 8-mile barrier of prickly pear cactus along the 17-mile fence, called the Cactus Curtain, to stop people crossing to the base.

Since 2002 the base has held a detention camp for people captured in the US war on terror. Because the final title lies with Cuba, a legal question arose as to whether US courts reached the base. In Boumediene v. Bush in 2008 the US Supreme Court ruled that detainees there have a constitutional right to challenge their detention in court. The split between title and control therefore did not put the base outside the US Constitution.

The base still operates, and Cuba still objects. The holder here is a powerful government with a military base on the land, and the owner's objection since 1959 has not changed who controls it.

hong-kong-new-territories-lease.story:
The New Territories are the mainland and island part of Hong Kong, leased by Britain from China in 1898 for 99 years with no rent. Hong Kong was built up in three steps. Britain took Hong Kong Island in 1842 after the First Opium War, and the Kowloon Peninsula in 1860 after the Second, both given up by China in perpetuity, meaning forever. The third step was different in law, since it was a lease with an end date.

In 1898, after China's defeat by Japan, Germany, Russia, France and Britain each pressed China for leases of coastal land, and Germany took Kiautschou Bay for 99 years that spring. Britain wanted land to defend its isolated colony, along with space for troop exercises and development. On 9 June it signed the Second Convention of Peking, covering the land north of what is now Boundary Street up to the Sham Chun River, along with New Kowloon and 235 islands. Under British law at the time, 99 years was the longest lease allowed. The treaty is often described as an unequal one, meaning it was forced on a weaker state. The Kowloon Walled City was left out and stayed under China.

Britain ran the leased land as part of the colony. Only the New Territories had to be returned, because they alone were under a lease. By the 1980s, though, the island and Kowloon had few resources of their own and large developments stood on the leased land, so splitting them off was seen as impractical.

Britain and the People's Republic of China negotiated in advance, and under their 1984 Joint Declaration all of Hong Kong, including the parts ceded permanently, passed to China. The handover took place at midnight on 30 June 1997, ending British rule after 156 years.

For anyone hoping to found a territory on leased land, this case shows that a long lease does end, and that the end date can pull the rest of the territory along with it. Britain negotiated 13 years ahead of the date, because of what stood on the leased land.

nasseri-charles-de-gaulle.story:
Mehran Karimi Nasseri was an Iranian man who lived in the departure lounge of Terminal 1 at Charles de Gaulle Airport near Paris from 26 August 1988 until July 2006, almost 18 years. Airports have a transit area, where travellers between international flights wait without passing immigration or customs, but such an area is fully under the law of the country where it sits. A person who breaks the law there can be prosecuted by that country.

Nasseri was born in 1945 in an oil company town in Iran and studied in Britain at the University of Bradford. He said he had been expelled from Iran in 1977 for protesting against the Shah, a claim later investigation disputed, and that after a long battle the UN refugee agency in Belgium gave him refugee status, which allowed him to live in other European countries. In 1988 he travelled towards Britain and his papers disappeared. He said they were stolen, and other accounts say he mailed them to Brussels from the ferry. Britain sent him back to France because he had no passport. At the French airport he could not prove who he was or what his status was, and he was detained in the waiting area.

Without papers he had no way to enter France. Lawyers argued over his status for years while he lived on a bench in the terminal. Belgium granted him residency in 1995 and France in 1999. He then refused to sign the papers, because they listed him as Iranian and did not use the name he had chosen, "Sir, Alfred Mehran". So by the end the legal block had gone, and he stayed by his own decision.

He stayed until he was taken to hospital in 2006, then lived in Paris shelters for 16 years. He returned to the airport in September 2022 and died there of a heart attack two months later. His autobiography appeared in 2004, and his story inspired the 2004 film The Terminal.

He never claimed the terminal as a separate place, and nobody treated it as one. His stay gave him no separate legal status. It shows what happens to a person without papers in a place that belongs to a state and offers him no way in.

panama-canal-zone.story:
The Panama Canal Zone was a strip of 1,432 square kilometres across Panama that the United States governed from 1903 to 1979. It covered the canal and land about five miles either side of its centre line, and left out the cities of Panama City and Colón.

The United States wanted a canal so that its warships could move between oceans, a need made clear in the Spanish-American War of 1898, when warships in the Atlantic had to reach battles in the Pacific. A French firm had already failed at the job. Panama was then part of Colombia. When the Colombian Senate held out for better terms in 1903, President Theodore Roosevelt's government gave covert support to rebels in Panama and protected them when they declared independence that November. The treaty signed on 18 November by Philippe Bunau-Varilla, a Frenchman acting for the new republic, let the United States build the canal. The Isthmian Canal Convention proclaimed in 1904 gave it use, occupation and control of a zone in perpetuity, which means with no end date. The United States also bought out the land from its private and public owners.

The zone had its own governor, police, courts and judges, including a US district court, and its capital at Balboa, and US dollars as currency, with the Panamanian balboa tolerated. Almost everyone worked for the canal company or the government. Residents did not own their homes. They rented houses assigned mainly by seniority, and they bought goods at stores run by the company. The residents were known as Zonians.

The zone cut Panama in two, and that caused growing conflict, with rioting in 1958, 1959 and January 1964, after which Panamanian flags were allowed to fly beside American ones. Years of negotiation led to the Torrijos-Carter Treaties of 1977, which passed the US Senate although polls showed only 23 percent of Americans in favour. The zone was abolished on 1 October 1979, and the canal itself was run jointly until it passed fully to Panama on 31 December 1999.

The grant in perpetuity therefore lasted 75 years. The legal text did not stop the two countries from replacing it by a further treaty, after decades of unrest over the zone.

snowden-sheremetyevo.story:
Edward Snowden, an American who leaked secret documents about US surveillance, spent about a month in the transit area of Sheremetyevo Airport in Moscow in 2013. A transit area is the part of an airport where travellers wait between international flights without passing through immigration. It can look like a place outside any country, and it is not, as Russian law applied there the whole time.

The United States charged him under the Espionage Act of 1917 and with theft of government property, and asked Hong Kong to hold him. Hong Kong said the request did not fully meet its law and let him go. On 23 June he flew to Moscow with Sarah Harrison of WikiLeaks. WikiLeaks said he was heading for asylum in Ecuador, and he held an Ecuadorian emergency travel document.

He had a seat booked on an onward flight to Cuba, which he did not take. The State Department revoked his passport, and accounts differ on when and why this stranded him. Snowden said the United States wanted him to stay in Moscow so that it could call him a Russian spy. The journalist Glenn Greenwald said the passport was cancelled during the flight, so that he could not buy a ticket onward. The Russian newspaper Kommersant reported that Cuba had told Moscow it would not let the plane land, after American pressure.

Without a passport he could not board another flight, and he could not enter Russia without its agreement. President Vladimir Putin said he was in the transit area, had committed no crime in Russia and was free to leave. WikiLeaks announced that he had applied for asylum in several more countries. On 23 July the US Attorney General wrote to Russia's justice minister offering a limited passport good only for a direct return to the United States, and promising that Snowden would not face torture or the death penalty.

About a month after he landed, Russia granted him asylum and he entered the country. On 26 September 2022 Putin granted him Russian citizenship. He became president of the Freedom of the Press Foundation, a San Francisco nonprofit, in 2016.

An airport corridor gave him no independent standing. What he could do next was decided by Russian officials, by the American cancellation of his passport, and by the countries at the other end of each possible flight.

un-headquarters-zones.mechanism: An international body can run its own premises inside a country, but most of that country's law continues to apply there, and the arrangement lasts only as long as the host agrees.
un-headquarters-zones.story:
The United Nations runs its headquarters in New York and its offices in Geneva, Vienna and Nairobi as a kind of international concession, meaning an area inside a country where another body has been given some authority. Most local and national law still applies in them.

The arrangement exists for a practical reason. Delegates from every member country must be able to attend meetings, including those whose governments are on bad terms with the host. So the host country agrees on special entry rules. The United States has a special visa, the C-2, which lets foreign officials who would otherwise be barred enter the country, on condition that they stay near the headquarters.

Countries have made similar deals with each other. The Tomb of Suleyman Shah, grandfather of the founder of the Ottoman Empire, lies in northern Syria and was made a Turkish concession by the Treaty of Ankara in 1921. The tomb was moved in 1973 because the new Euphrates Lake would flood the site. In 2015 Turkey moved it again on its own because of the Syrian civil war. Syria called that move incompatible with the 1921 treaty, and Turkey has said it plans to return the tomb to its second site.

The Tangier International Zone in Morocco was a larger example, a concession of 373 square kilometres run by a group of foreign powers from 1923 to 1956, with its own legislative assembly. It ended when Morocco regained full sovereignty. Each of these rested on an agreement with the state whose land it was.

asgardia.story:
Asgardia is a self-declared space nation run from Vienna, Austria, whose only territory has been one small satellite. The Russian engineer Igor Ashurbeyli, who had founded a space research centre in Vienna in 2013, announced it at a press conference in Paris on 12 October 2016. The name comes from Asgard, the home of the gods in Norse myth.

The reason given for the project is a real feature of space law. The Outer Space Treaty of 1967 requires governments to authorise and supervise everything their citizens and companies do in space. Asgardia's backers wanted access to space free of existing nations, and they reasoned that if they became a nation themselves, they could escape those restrictions. They said they would apply to the United Nations and aimed at a settlement on the Moon by 2043. Members were not expected to move into space.

People could join online. Over 100,000 applied within two days and 500,000 within three weeks, though tougher checks cut the figure to about 210,000 by June 2017. A constitution passed that month, with no formal way to vote against it, and made the state a kingdom with Ashurbeyli at its head, a 150-seat parliament and a court. It names a planned cryptocurrency called the Solar. Parliament met in Vienna, and Ashurbeyli was inaugurated at the Hofburg palace on 25 June 2018. He was re-elected with 93.17 percent in September 2022.

On 12 November 2017 a Cygnus cargo spacecraft, launched by an Antares rocket from Virginia, released the satellite Asgardia-1, weighing 2.8 kilograms, into orbit. Asgardia then called itself the first nation with all its territory in space. Legal scholars disagreed, for reasons that show how the law works. American companies launched the satellite on a NASA-funded mission, so the United States was the launching state and had to answer for it. Article VIII of the treaty keeps legal authority over a spacecraft with the country that registers it, and Article II bars anyone from claiming space. A satellite is therefore a piece of property under some country's law, and it gives its owners no territory.

The satellite burned up in the atmosphere on 12 September 2022, and no replacement has been reported. A press release from Asgardia reports a congress in Dubai on 30 October 2025 and claims over one million citizens. No state or UN body recognises it, and no one has ever lived there.

aurora-station.story:
Aurora Station was a proposed hotel in orbit from Orion Span, a startup in Houston, Texas, led by the former software engineer Frank Bunger. Announced in April 2018, it was to be a single module 35 feet long and 14 feet wide, about as roomy inside as a Gulfstream G550 business jet, circling 200 miles above Earth with four guests and two crew.

The offer was to sell the experience of being an astronaut. A 12-day stay would cost $9.5 million per person, or about $790,000 a night, and a refundable $80,000 deposit held a place. Guests would see 384 sunrises and sunsets on the trip. Launch was planned for late 2021, with guests the following year. The company said its top technical staff came from NASA, but it would not say how much money it needed. It signed no launch contract and never started construction.

An archived copy of its website said in March 2021 that operations had stopped and deposits had been refunded, while a later radio report gave 2022 as the year it closed. The company never claimed sovereignty, and it shut down before any regulator had to decide who would govern guests on board. Had it flown, an American company would have needed American authorisation and supervision, under Article VI of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty. The obstacle that ended it was money, well before the law on private hotels in orbit came into play.

bigelow-aerospace.story:
Bigelow Aerospace was an American company in North Las Vegas, Nevada, that built inflatable modules for living in space. An inflatable module launches folded and expands in orbit, which makes it roomier and lighter than a rigid one. Robert Bigelow, who had made his money from the Budget Suites of America hotel chain, founded the company in 1998 and paid for it himself.

NASA had worked on the idea in a project called TransHab, which Congress cancelled in the late 1990s because of delays and budget limits. In 2000 Bigelow licensed the technology. It flew two uncrewed prototypes, Genesis I and II, in 2006 and 2007. In December 2012 NASA signed a $17.8 million contract for an expandable module called BEAM, which was added to the International Space Station in April 2016. By 2013 Bigelow had put in $250 million of his own money, and he said he would spend up to about $500 million. In 2010 it announced plans for a modular set of space habitats for creating or expanding stations.

Article VI of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty requires the United States to authorise and supervise its companies in space, and the company sought clear rules for private stations from regulators. In 2014 the Federal Aviation Administration, which licenses rocket launches, wrote to Bigelow saying it could use its existing review of a launch's payload to cover such missions. Lawyers at the group TechFreedom criticised this as having no clear limits. A private habitat would therefore still need American permission.

In March 2020 Bigelow laid off all 88 staff and blamed the COVID-19 pandemic. When its engineering contract with NASA ended, NASA took ownership of BEAM, which remains in use on the station. The company was described as defunct as of January 2024. Nobody ever lived on its free-flying modules. The one module people could enter passed to a government agency.

cloud-constellation-spacebelt.story:
SpaceBelt was a plan by Cloud Constellation Corporation of Los Angeles to store customers' data on satellites in low Earth orbit and pass it between them, so that it never crossed the public internet or any country's land networks. It would use a ring of 10 satellites, 650 kilometres up over the equator, linked by lasers and reached from the ground through small dish terminals. This would make it an orbital data haven, a place to keep information out of reach of national rules.

The company was founded in 2015. Its marketing said it would sidestep laws on how data moves between countries. Its president Cliff Beek pitched hosting data without wrangling over international compliance, and in 2017 the company offered it as an answer to GDPR, the European Union's data protection rules. Trade reporters pointed out that those rules protect European residents' data even when it is processed outside the EU, so moving the data does not remove the duty.

The legal claim has a further weakness. Under the Outer Space Treaty, the launching and registering country keeps legal authority over a satellite and answers for what its companies do there. An American company with customers on the ground would remain within reach of courts and regulators, through the company itself and through its terminals.

The money problem came first. The company raised $5 million in 2016 and said it needed $480 million to reach orbit. In December 2018 it announced a $100 million commitment from HCH Group of Hong Kong. In November 2019 CFIUS, the US panel that reviews foreign investment, raised problems with that money because HCH is a Chinese company. So a US government panel stood in the way of the funding for a project pitched as beyond national rules. By April 2020 no replacement funding had been announced, and that month the company announced a benchmark test with IBM, with service planned for 2022. No launch has been reported, and no news of the project since 2020.

fcc-starlink-licensing.story:
Outer space belongs to no country, yet a national telecoms regulator can set rules for what happens there. To see why, start with what a satellite needs. It must send radio signals to the ground, and to sell a service it must have customers on the ground. Radio frequencies are licensed by governments, working within the international system run by the International Telecommunication Union. So a regulator that controls access to customers has a hold over the satellite, even though the satellite itself sits in a place no country may claim.

The US Federal Communications Commission (FCC) decides who may use radio frequencies to reach customers in the United States. In a 2018 order it allowed SpaceX to run a system of 4,425 satellites offering broadband internet around the world, under its Starlink plan,. Under Article VI of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, the United States must authorise and supervise its companies in space, and in practice the FCC does much of this for SpaceX.

The FCC has also shown that it can punish a company for what it leaves in orbit. In 2002 Dish Network launched a satellite called EchoStar-7 into geostationary orbit, the band 36,000 kilometres up where a satellite appears to hang over one spot on Earth. In 2012 Dish agreed to move it 186 miles higher at the end of its life, into a graveyard orbit out of the way of working satellites. In February 2022, low on fuel, it managed only about 76 miles. On 2 October 2023 the FCC announced its first fine for space debris. Dish admitted liability, paid $150,000 and accepted a compliance plan. The enforcement chief called this a breakthrough settlement showing the agency's strong authority.

A company that wants customers on the ground stays within reach of the regulator that licenses its signals. Anyone planning a separate community in orbit would meet the same regulator when trying to send signals to people on Earth or sell to them. Starlink's own 2020 beta terms made California law govern service on Earth and the Moon.

flags-of-convenience-space.story:
A flag of convenience is a practice from shipping. Every merchant ship must be registered in a country and fly its flag, and that country's law then applies on board. Owners can choose to register in a country with light rules and low fees, even one the ship never visits. Lawyers have asked whether spacecraft can do the same, since a spacecraft also has a country of registry, under the UN Registration Convention and Article VIII of the Outer Space Treaty.

Adrian Taghdiri wrote a 2013 note in the Boston University Journal of Science and Technology Law, as space tourism was starting, predicting that some countries would set loose rules to attract private space companies. He warned of environmental harm, more debris and danger to passengers. He also argued that some states might ignore the penalties the treaty places on them for their private actors.

Space law limits the effect without removing it. The registering country keeps legal authority over a spacecraft and its crew. But a launching state, meaning a country that launches a craft, pays for its launch, or lets its soil be used, stays liable for damage under Article VII. So a cheap registry could lighten the rules that a company lives under, but it cannot remove the responsibility of the country where the rocket went up.

A presentation at a symposium of the UN's space law subcommittee in Vienna in 2016 set out the shipping idea and asked how it fits space objects. The closest working example involves orbital slots, the positions assigned to satellites. Tonga, a small Pacific kingdom, has a company called Tongasat, whose business of holding slots has been described as in effect a flag of convenience for space. Later filings of the kind came from Gibraltar, Papua New Guinea and Bermuda.

The practice has not been tested in any court,. Choosing a light-touch registry might reduce supervision, but it would not produce independence, because the treaty keeps some state's law attached to every registered craft.

iss-intergovernmental-agreement.story:
The International Space Station orbits Earth with people living on it and has no government of its own. A treaty signed on 29 January 1998 by the United States, Canada, Japan, Russia and member countries of the European Space Agency divides legal authority among them.

Under Article 5, each partner keeps legal control over the modules it registers and over its own citizens on board. So the station works a little like a building where each floor belongs to a different country. The European Space Agency describes the modules as treated like part of the partners' territory, so European law applies inside Europe's Columbus laboratory, and national courts hear cases on liability and inventions. Special rules cover inventions made there, to prevent simultaneous claims in several European countries.

Crime has its own rule, in Article 22. A Congressional Research Service paper explains that each country may prosecute its own citizens for what they do in any module. If the misconduct endangers another country's citizen, or happens in or damages another partner's module, the suspect's country must consult the affected country. The affected country may then prosecute if the suspect's country agrees or gives no assurance that it will prosecute.

Daily order rests on a Crew Code of Conduct agreed in September 2000, which sets a chain of command for the astronauts and cosmonauts. Below the treaty sit four agreements between NASA and each other space agency, and further detailed arrangements.

The station is still in orbit under these rules, with seven people on board in early November 2026. Each partner's law applies in its own modules, and no single legal authority covers the whole station. People have lived there under this treaty without creating a new territory. It extended existing national law outward, one module at a time.

kessler-limits.mechanism: Debris crosses every orbit, so activity there cannot be physically separated. That limits how exclusive any claim to a place in orbit can be, and it makes each operator depend on all the others.
kessler-limits.story:
Kessler syndrome is a predicted chain reaction of collisions in orbit, and it places a physical limit on any plan to live or build there. In June 1978 the NASA scientists Donald Kessler and Burton Cour-Palais published a paper called "Collision Frequency of Artificial Satellites: The Creation of a Debris Belt". Kessler and Cour-Palais showed that if low Earth orbit became crowded enough, collisions would create debris, and that debris would cause more collisions, without anyone launching anything further.

Kessler reached this by applying to satellite records a method developed for studying the asteroid belt. He found that 42 percent of catalogued debris came from 19 events, mainly explosions of spent rocket stages when leftover fuel burst their tanks. At the time many people thought drag from the thin upper atmosphere would clear debris faster than it formed. In 2009 Kessler wrote that modelling showed the environment had already become unstable, so that fragments from future collisions would pile up faster than drag could remove them, even with no new debris sources. By 2025 there were an estimated 11,800 satellites in orbit, of which 7,135 belonged to Starlink, and the chain reaction becomes likelier as the number grows.

This bears on any claim to a place in orbit, because a settlement cannot fence off its surroundings. One operator's debris endangers all the others. A would-be orbital nation would depend on the conduct of every operator around it and would have no power over them.

No treaty sets a limit on debris, so the rules are national. The US Federal Communications Commission now requires satellites to be disposed of within five years of the end of their mission, and its 2023 fine against Dish Network is an early case of one country enforcing its own debris rules. In the worst case, some orbital regions would become unusable for many generations.

mircorp.story:
MirCorp was a company based in Amsterdam that tried to turn the aging Russian space station Mir into a private business. The Russian space company RSC Energia, a major shareholder in MirCorp, was behind the plan to keep the station in orbit.

The driving figure was the American telecoms millionaire Walt Anderson, thought to be the main source of its first money, who heard that Energia might sell, flew to Russia with a team and made a deal. Its president was Jeffrey Manber. Energia authorised MirCorp to lease Mir for tourism, advertising, industry and science for the rest of the station's life. Commercial use was priced at $10 million to $20 million. So this was a lease of operating rights, on a station that stayed Russian.

NASA's head Dan Goldin said he was not pleased, because the plan drew Russian attention and money away from the International Space Station. On 4 April 2000 MirCorp paid for the flight Soyuz TM-30, which carried Sergei Zalyotin and Aleksandr Kaleri to repair and restart the station. They were the last crew Mir ever received, and for that time it was in effect the first commercial space station. The company signed up Dennis Tito as a paying passenger and said it had $100 million in future business, including a planned reality show. Those involved later described tourism as a fallback.

The plan needed a tether from the United States to raise the station's orbit. Exporting it required approval under ITAR, the US rules on sending space and defence technology abroad, and the approval arrived too late. Its money ran out when the dot-com crash hit Anderson's investments. Manber said the company failed for lack of about $10 million. Some of its supporters argue that the US government wanted to stop any rival to its own station.

Mir was brought down from orbit in March 2001. Tito flew to the International Space Station that year instead. Anderson later pleaded guilty to tax evasion and was sentenced to nine years in prison. A private lease controlled little here. Launch, law, export licences and the station's own fate stayed with governments, and any one of them could stop the venture.

nasa-commercial-stations.story:
NASA plans to replace the International Space Station with privately owned stations in low Earth orbit, where it would rent space. Under its Commercial Low Earth Orbit Destinations program, in December 2021 NASA gave three teams a total of $415.6 million.

Orbital Reef, announced by Blue Origin in October 2021 with Boeing and Sierra Space, later had its award raised to $172 million. Starlab, from Voyager Space, was raised to $217.5 million after Northrop Grumman joined it, and it later became a Voyager and Airbus venture. Axiom Space holds a separate fixed-price contract. Axiom plans to attach its first module to the existing station and then fly on its own as early as 2028. Starlab aims for 2029. A National Space Society summary says Orbital Reef remains in various stages of planning.

A second funding round was meant to pick winners by April 2026, but on 28 January 2026 NASA put it on hold to match revised requirements. It issued a draft request for proposals in July 2026, and an industry report of 24 September said no award had been made.

The legal position is clear enough. Under Article VI of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, the United States must authorise and keep supervising its companies in space, and each company would also need licences for launch and radio. All three depend on the US government as main customer and funder, which gives it a further hold through its contracts. None of the three seeks to govern itself, and none has flown.

orbis-lease-salter.story:
The ORBIS lease is a model contract for a privately owned settlement in space, discussed in a 2019 article by Alexander Salter of Texas Tech University in the United States. The article, in the Journal of Air Law and Commerce, starts from Article II of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, which forbids any country from claiming territory in space. If no state can extend its territory there, Salter argues, the rules for human conduct in space must come from somewhere other than states.

His answer is the proprietary community, a settlement owned and run privately, whose residents accept its rules by contract. Salter surveys the reasons such communities are likely to supply good governance, and then looks at the lease called ORBIS, drawn up by Spencer MacCallum, a scholar of such communities. Salter argues that this voluntary model would be expected to work better than others.

The difficulty is the next article of the same treaty. Article VI says that countries bear international responsibility for what private groups do in space, and that private activity needs authorisation and continuing supervision by a state. Critics of private claims in space, including writers on SpaceX's terms of service, point to this rule. A lease does not end the duty of the home country. There is a further question about what a private owner owns. Article VIII protects ownership of objects built in space, while Article II bars national claims to the ground.

No settlement is known to have used the lease, and it remains a proposal on paper.
