swarm-spacebees-fcc.story:
Swarm Technologies is an American satellite company founded in 2016 by Sara Spangelo and Benjamin Longmier, and it launched its first satellites without permission. The company used very small satellites, each a quarter of the smallest standard size, known as 0.25U. Their small size was the source of the dispute.

In April 2017 it asked the US Federal Communications Commission (FCC) for an experimental licence to run four such satellites, called SpaceBEEs, and two ground stations. In December 2017 the FCC refused, because it feared satellites so small could not be tracked and could become invisible debris. Swarm launched them anyway on 12 January 2018, on an Indian rocket that also carried other satellites.

The launch was on foreign soil, which might suggest the FCC had no say. But the agency reached the company by other routes. Swarm was an American company, and its satellites had sent signals to ground stations in Georgia in the United States for more than a week. The agency also found unauthorised tests from weather balloons. After reports of the launch surfaced, it opened an investigation in March 2018 and warned the whole industry not to arrange launches after a licence had been refused.

In December 2018 Swarm signed a consent decree, a settlement enforced by the regulator. It paid a $900,000 penalty to the US Treasury, accepted a strict compliance plan and agreed to file pre-launch reports for three years. It then made its satellites larger and easier to track, which won it a licence. SpaceX bought the company for $524 million in 2021, and its service was shut down by 2025.

For anyone thinking of launching from a foreign site to avoid a home regulator, this case gives a direct answer. The foreign launch did not help, because the company and its ground stations were within American reach.

vast-haven-1.story:
Haven-1 is a small private space station being built in Long Beach, California, by the American company Vast, led by chief executive Max Haot. Announced in 2023, it is a single module of about 14 tons with about 45 cubic metres of living space. It is planned to orbit at 425 kilometres for about three years and would be the first fully commercial station if it flies.

It cannot support people on its own for long. It depends on a docked SpaceX Crew Dragon capsule for life support, up to 1,000 watts of power and up to 150 kilograms of cargo. Crews of four would stay for up to 30 days by one account and up to two weeks by another. They would carry out research and in-space manufacturing. So the people on board are short-stay customers who arrive and leave on another company's spacecraft.

In early 2026 Vast moved the launch from 2026 to no earlier than the first quarter of 2027, on a Falcon 9 rocket, and Haot said in September 2026 that this date still held. Crewed flights depend on SpaceX agreeing that it is safe to dock, which Haot told Ars Technica could happen two weeks after launch or at any time in the station's three-year life. Vast's larger Haven-2 is meant to keep a crew aboard continuously after the International Space Station retires.

Vast makes no claim to sovereignty. Article VI of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty requires the United States to authorise and supervise its companies in space, and it would also need licences for launch and for radio. Haven-1 would be private property in a place no country may claim, with an American company answerable to American regulators. Haven-1 had not been launched as of November 2026.

add_sources.t: Outer Space Treaty, full text (UN Office for Outer Space Affairs)

voyager-station.story:
Voyager Station was a proposed hotel in orbit, shaped like a rotating wheel, announced by the Gateway Foundation of California in 2019 under the name Von Braun Station. Rotation would press people against the outer rim and imitate gravity, and the rocket engineer Wernher von Braun drew designs for rotating stations in the 1950s. It would have 24 modules joined by elevator shafts and be fully working by 2027.

Two years later CNN reported the new name and a builder, Orbital Assembly Corporation, run by the former pilot John Blincow, who also headed the foundation. Publicity promised regular beds, showers, bars and restaurants. Orbital Assembly's design architect Tim Alatorre said in 2019 that the eventual goal was a starship culture of people living and working in space. Reports describe it as a hotel and say nothing of separate government or legal status.

Orbital Assembly was later renamed Above: Space Development Corporation, and as of 2024 it had announced no funding for its stations and had not begun construction. Its situation in 2026 is unknown, and it was not among the commercial stations named in a National Space Society summary of that year. The station has not been built.

Because it never reached a launch or licence application, no authority had to rule on it. An American company building such a station would need US authorisation under Article VI of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, along with launch and radio licences. None of those steps had been taken as of 2024.

add_sources.t: Outer Space Treaty, full text (UN Office for Outer Space Affairs)

curiosity.story:
Curiosity is a car-sized NASA rover exploring Gale crater and Mount Sharp on Mars. It landed on 6 August 2012 on the crater floor, at a spot named Bradbury Landing, to study the planet's climate and geology and whether ancient Mars could have supported life. These coordinates mark that landing point. It has kept working well beyond its planned two years and has driven more than 36 kilometres, so its real position keeps changing.

A moving machine on another planet raises the question of whose law applies to it and what happens to the ground it crosses. The answer comes from the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, the main international agreement on space. Article VIII says the country that registers a spacecraft keeps "jurisdiction and control" over it, meaning the power to make and apply law to it. So the United States keeps control of the rover wherever it goes.

That authority stops at the machine. Article II bars any country from claiming land on another world, "by means of use or occupation, or by any other means". A rover has now used the same stretch of ground for over a decade, and that gives its owner no rights to the land. Anyone hoping that long use of a place on Mars would turn into a title has this rule to get past.

insight.story:
InSight was a NASA lander that studied the deep interior of Mars from Elysium Planitia, a plain near the planet's equator. It landed on 26 November 2018 and carried a seismometer, an instrument that detects ground shaking, and a heat probe. It confirmed marsquakes, which showed that the inside of the planet is still active. Its last contact was on 15 December 2022, and NASA declared the mission over six days later. Its instruments are still in place on the ground.

A dead spacecraft keeps its legal status. Article VIII of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, the main international agreement on space, says a spacecraft stays under the legal authority of the country that registered it, and that ownership of objects "landed or constructed on a celestial body" is not affected by their presence there. There is no rule that a machine left silent for years becomes abandoned. So InSight still belongs to the United States.

Read plainly, a later visitor who wanted to move it or take it apart would need American consent, and any future settlement on Mars would have to treat old landers as other countries' property. No case has tested this.

mars-3.story:
Mars 3 was a Soviet probe that made the first soft landing on Mars, in the Terra Sirenum region, on 2 December 1971. It failed 110 seconds after landing, having sent only a grey image with no detail, possibly because of a huge dust storm raging at the time. The lander carried a small rover called PrOP-M. Its coordinates here are an estimate.

The 1967 Outer Space Treaty, the main international agreement on space, was already in force. Article VIII says that landing on another world does not change who owns a spacecraft, and it keeps legal authority with the country that registered it.

This case tests that rule twice. The first test is failure. The lander worked for less than two minutes, and it is still property. The second is the end of the country itself. The Soviet Union dissolved in 1991, and Russia is treated as its continuing state. Ownership of the lander therefore passes to Russia, 20 years after it stopped working.

For anyone planning a long-lived settlement, it shows that a country's rights over an object can outlast the government that sent it. It also leaves a question unanswered. The treaty does not say what happens when a state disappears without a clear successor, and no case on another planet has tested it.

mars-one.story:
Mars One was a small Dutch venture that planned a permanent human colony on Mars with volunteers on a one-way trip, paid for partly by a reality television show. Its chief executive Bas Lansdorp announced it in 2012.

It had two parts, a nonprofit foundation and a for-profit company, Mars One Ventures, with very few staff. It was not an aerospace firm and meant to buy rockets, spacecraft, habitats and suits from outside suppliers, at an estimated $6 billion for the first mission. Early plans sent robots first in 2020 and settlers a few years later, and by 2019 the target had slipped to 2031.

The company said 202,586 people from about 140 countries applied in 2013. Joseph Roche, a physicist among the finalists, said only 2,761 had completed the process, and the company later confirmed his figure. Roche and others called it a scam, which it denied, and academics called the plan a suicide mission. Contracts for early design studies with Lockheed Martin and Surrey Satellite Technology ran out.

On 15 January 2019 the Civil Court of Basel in Switzerland declared Mars One Ventures bankrupt, with debts of about 1 million euros, and an appeal failed. Lansdorp said the foundation was untouched, but the bankrupt company was the part meant to raise money. No hardware was built.

The law on Mars was never reached. Had a launch gone ahead, the registering country would have kept legal authority over the craft and its crew under the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, and a state would have had to authorise the one-way mission. The project ended instead in a Swiss court, over debts of about 1 million euros, far below the $6 billion estimated for the mission.

add_sources.t: Outer Space Treaty, full text (UN Office for Outer Space Affairs)

mars-society-city-state.story:
The Mars Society is an American volunteer nonprofit, funded by donations, that lobbies for human missions to Mars. The engineer Robert Zubrin, founded it on 13 August 1998 at a convention of 750 people in Boulder, Colorado.

All its physical work has been on Earth. It runs analogue stations, meaning simulated Mars bases, on Devon Island in the Canadian Arctic and in the desert at its Mars Desert Research Station. Crews live there under mission rules for weeks or months, including an 80-day stay in 2017.

It has also asked how a society on Mars would be organised. In 2019 it held a contest to design a colony of 1,000, won by a Massachusetts Institute of Technology team with a plan called Star City, made up of five starting villages. In 2020 it announced a second contest for a city state of one million people, with a $10,000 prize. A city state is a single city that rules itself as a country. Zubrin's 2024 book The New World on Mars predicts populous Martian city-states with governments of the people that draw immigrants from Earth, paying for imports through enterprises such as real estate.

These designs have no legal force, and the society has adopted no known constitution for Mars. The law as it stands points in another direction. The 1967 Outer Space Treaty bars any country from claiming land there, and it makes each country responsible for its citizens' activities in space. So a settlement on Mars would begin as an activity supervised by some country on Earth. How such a settlement could move to self-rule under the treaty has not been settled.

add_sources.t: Outer Space Treaty, full text (UN Office for Outer Space Affairs)

perseverance.story:
Perseverance is a car-sized NASA rover that landed in Jezero crater on Mars on 18 February 2021, at the point marked here. The crater was chosen because its ancient river delta may hold signs of past life. The rover has been driving and collecting rock and soil samples ever since, sealing them in tubes, and it has left some sealed tubes on the surface for a later mission to bring back. NASA paused its plan for that return in 2023 over its cost and turned to industry and its Jet Propulsion Laboratory for a cheaper design.

The tubes raise a legal point that most landers do not. They sit on the ground, separate from the rover, perhaps for many years. Article VIII of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, the main international agreement on space, says the registering country keeps legal authority over a spacecraft, and that ownership of objects "and of their component parts" is not affected by being in space or by returning to Earth. So the tubes remain American as they lie on Mars. Article VIII also says that such objects found elsewhere must be returned to the registering country.

The Martian rock inside the tubes is a harder question. Article II bars countries from claiming land on Mars, and the treaty does not say plainly whether a piece of rock removed from the ground can be owned. The United States and others in the Artemis Accords, a set of non-binding principles, say that extracting resources is not in itself a claim to territory. If a founder hoped to make use of local rock and ice, that is the unsettled rule they would meet.

add_sources.t: Artemis Accords (Wikipedia)

phoenix.story:
Phoenix was a NASA lander that came down in the Green Valley of Vastitas Borealis, in the far north of Mars, on 25 May 2008. It was the first NASA mission to land in the planet's polar region, and it went there to study water and whether the area could have supported life. It operated for 157 Martian days until the winter cut its solar power, and its last contact was on 2 November 2008.

The lander is still there. Article VIII of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, the main international agreement on space, keeps legal authority with the United States as the registering country, and landing does not change who owns the machine.

The site gives the United States no claim to the plain, because Article II bars claims to land on other worlds. Article XII adds that stations and equipment on a celestial body are open to representatives of other treaty members on a basis of reciprocity, with reasonable notice. Article IX tells countries to act with due regard for others and to avoid harmful contamination. So an owner keeps the machine, and the treaty gives it no right to close off the region around it.

starlink-mars-free-planet.story:
In October 2020 SpaceX, the American rocket company, put an unusual sentence in the terms of service for the early test of its Starlink internet service. Terms of service are a contract between a company and its customers, and they usually say which law settles any dispute. Under this section, service on Earth or the Moon fell under California law. The next sentence read: "For Services provided on Mars, or in transit to Mars via Starship or other colonization spacecraft, the parties recognize Mars as a free planet and that no Earth-based government has authority or sovereignty over Martian activities." Disputes there would be settled by self-governing principles agreed at the time of settlement.

Because it mentions colonization spacecraft, the sentence was read as a statement about how a future colony would be run.

Lawyers replied quickly. An article in Völkerrechtsblog, an international law blog, pointed to Article VI of the Outer Space Treaty, under which the United States must authorise and supervise SpaceX's actions in space. In practice the US Federal Communications Commission does this through its licences. The article argued that SpaceX cannot opt out of this, that its conduct in space counts as that of the United States, and that such a claim risks breaching Article II, the ban on claiming land in space. A law journal note at the University of Richmond said the clause tried to sidestep international law.

The legal point is about who is bound. A contract binds the people who sign it. A customer and SpaceX can agree between themselves on how to settle a dispute. They cannot by contract release a government from a treaty it has signed, or take away powers that a government has and neither of them gave it. So the clause could at most affect a claim between the customer and the company.

No one has yet reached Mars under these terms, and no court has ruled on it. It is not known whether the clause remains in Starlink's current terms.

add_sources.t: Outer Space Treaty, full text (UN Office for Outer Space Affairs)

viking-1.story:
Viking 1 was the NASA lander that became the first successful spacecraft on the surface of Mars. It touched down on the plain of Chryse Planitia on 20 July 1976 and sent back the first clear image from the surface. An earlier Soviet lander, Mars 3, had reached the surface in 1971 but failed within two minutes. Viking 1 worked for about six years, until 11 November 1982, when a faulty command from the ground meant to update its battery software overwrote the data used to point its antenna, and contact was lost.

It still sits on the plain, and it is a useful test of the idea that being first gives rights. On Earth, explorers often claimed land for their rulers by arriving first. The 1967 Outer Space Treaty, the main international agreement on space, ended that for space. Article I says space is free for all countries to explore and use, and Article II bars any country from claiming land there by use, occupation or any other means.

Article VIII says the registering country keeps legal authority over a spacecraft and that landing does not change who owns it. So the United States still owns the machine. The plain did not become American, and a later arrival from any country has the same right to land there.

yemeni-mars-suit.story:
In 1997 three men in Yemen, Adam Ismail, Mustafa Khalil and Abdullah al-Umari, filed a complaint against NASA with Yemen's Prosecutor General, accusing the American space agency of invading Mars. At the time NASA's Pathfinder mission and its small rover Sojourner were sending back more than 1,000 pictures from the planet. The men told the Yemeni weekly Al-Thawri that the craft had landed and begun exploring without informing them or seeking their approval. They said they had inherited Mars from their ancestors 3,000 years earlier, and they based the claim on the mythologies of the Himyaritic and Sabaean civilisations of ancient Arabia.

The 1967 Outer Space Treaty had already barred countries from claiming land in space, and inheritance from ancient peoples has no place in that rule. The story comes from a popular history newsletter and Wikipedia, and no court record is known. The newsletter says the chief prosecutor rejected the petition and threatened the men with jail for wasting official time.

The claim came four years before Gregory Nemitz sent NASA a bill for parking on the asteroid Eros. A prosecutor in Yemen has no power over NASA or over land on Mars, and the case never reached a court.

add_sources.t: Outer Space Treaty, full text (UN Office for Outer Space Affairs)

zhurong.story:
Tianwen-1 was China's first mission to land on another planet. Its lander set down on the plain of Utopia Planitia on Mars on 14 May 2021, making China the third country to land softly there, and the Zhurong rover rolled off eight days later. Zhurong worked for 358 days, well past its planned 93, and went into planned hibernation on 18 May 2022 ahead of sandstorms and winter. It was due to wake in December 2022 but never did, because dust covered its solar panels. Both machines remain on the surface, and sources differ slightly on the exact position.

The case is useful because it shows that the rules on space apply the same way to rival powers. Article VIII of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, the main international agreement on space, gives China, as the registering country, legal authority over both machines, and landing does not change who owns them. Article II bars China from claiming the plain, just as it bars the United States from claiming the plains where its own landers sit.

So Mars holds machines belonging to several countries, each under its own country's authority, and the treaty is the only shared rule between them.

apollo-11.story:
Apollo 11 was the NASA mission that put the first people on the Moon, at Tranquility Base, in July 1969. Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin landed in the lunar module Eagle, and its lower half, the descent stage, still stands there with an American flag, instruments and their bootprints. The coordinates are NASA's, measured from images taken by its Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter.

The flag invites an obvious question. The 1967 Outer Space Treaty, the main international agreement on space, had taken effect two years before the landing. Article II bars any country from claiming the Moon by any means, so the flag gave the United States no title. The ground under it stays unclaimed.

Article VIII says the country that registers a spacecraft keeps legal authority over it and that landing does not change who owns it. That covers the hardware only. So the descent stage and flag are American property. The bootprints are marks on ground nobody owns, and that rule does not cover them.

This gap has led to efforts to protect the site. The group For All Moonkind argues that places like Tranquility Base are human heritage. It helped draft the US One Small Step Act, passed unanimously by the Senate in 2019, to turn NASA's preservation recommendations for Apollo sites into law. A national law of that kind reaches only those under US authority, and the treaty has no specific rule on heritage sites.

add_sources.t: For All Moonkind (Wikipedia)

apollo-17.story:
Apollo 17 was the last crewed NASA landing on the Moon, in December 1972, in a valley called Taurus-Littrow on the southeastern rim of Mare Serenitatis. Gene Cernan and Harrison Schmitt, a geologist, drove about 35.7 kilometres in a Lunar Roving Vehicle and brought back 110.52 kilograms of samples. The descent stage of their lander Challenger, the rover and a science package remain in the valley, and no one has landed there since.

Article VIII of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, the main international agreement on space, says the registering country keeps legal authority over its spacecraft and that landing does not change who owns them. There is no time limit. So the United States still owns the car and the rest of the hardware.

The same treaty leaves the valley unowned. Article II bars claims to land on the Moon, and the crew's stay gave no rights. The treaty does not explain how a country that cannot own the Moon comes to own rock taken from it. That question matters more now that the Artemis Accords and others discuss extracting resources.

add_sources.t: Artemis Accords (Wikipedia)

artemis-accords.story:
The Artemis Accords are a set of non-binding principles for civil activity on the Moon and beyond, drawn up by NASA and the US State Department to go with NASA's Artemis program of Moon missions. Non-binding means no country can be taken to court for breaking them. Eight countries signed on 13 October 2020: Australia, Canada, Italy, Japan, Luxembourg, the United Arab Emirates, the United Kingdom and the United States. According to NASA, Vietnam became the 78th signatory on 28 October 2026.

The background is a gap in the law. The Outer Space Treaty of 1967 bars countries from claiming land in space, and it guarantees free access to all areas. It also tells them to avoid harmful interference with one another. It does not say what happens when two missions want the same crater with ice in it. The Moon Agreement of 1979 tried to fill the gap by calling the Moon's resources the common heritage of humanity, to be managed under an international system. Only 18 countries ever joined.

The most debated part of the Accords is the safety zone. Signatories say they will announce where they are working and coordinate so that they do not interfere with each other. A zone covers an area where other operations could cause harmful interference. Its size and length depend on the work done there, and it ends when the work stops. Inside it, signatories say they still respect free access by others. NASA says this respects the treaty. The open question is how far a zone can go before it becomes the kind of claim the treaty forbids.

The Accords also say that extracting resources in space is possible before any further international rules exist, and that this is not in itself a claim to territory. A McGill University paper reads this as differing from the Moon Agreement, which calls for an international system first. Saudi Arabia signed the Accords in July 2022 and notified its withdrawal from the Moon Agreement six months later. The China-Russia lunar base project has been described as a rival.

No court has tested the zones. For a would-be founder, they show the most that current practice offers, which is a temporary priority at a place through use and notice, under a government's sponsorship, with no ownership. It lasts only as long as the work goes on.

blue-ghost-1.story:
Blue Ghost Mission 1 was a robotic Moon landing by Firefly Aerospace, an American private company, on a NASA-backed flight carrying ten experiments. It landed in Mare Crisium, near Mons Latreille, on 2 March 2025, and it is described as the first fully successful soft landing by a commercial company. It worked until the batteries ran down after sunset on 16 March.

Because the lander belongs to a company, it shows how the law treats private hardware. The 1967 Outer Space Treaty, the main international agreement on space, addresses private companies directly. Article VI makes the United States responsible for authorising and supervising its companies in space, and makes it answerable for what they do. Article VIII protects the company's ownership of the machine and leaves legal authority with the country that registered it.

The company gains no land. Article II bars national claims to the Moon,. So a private lander is private property under a government's supervision, standing on ground nobody owns.

celestia.story:
The Nation of Celestial Space, or Celestia, was a one-man claim to all of outer space by James Thomas Mangan, an American public relations man and writer from the Chicago area. He issued a declaration on 21 December 1948, and on 1 January 1949 he registered his claim with the Recorder of Deeds and Titles of Cook County, Illinois. A recorder of deeds is a local office that keeps copies of property documents. It records what people file and does not rule on whether they own what they say. He said he acted for humanity, to stop any one country from dominating space.

This was years before any satellite. The nation claimed 19 members at its foundation and 19,057 a decade later, while another source gives 100,000. In 1949 he told the United States, the Soviet Union, the United Kingdom and the United Nations that Celestia had banned further atmospheric nuclear tests.

When the space race began he sent letters of protest to the Soviet and American leaders about their flights crossing his territory, though he later waived this for satellite launches. In 1958 he applied to join the UN and raised his flag outside its New York headquarters. He issued stamps, gold and silver coins called Celestons, and passports, and he sent passports to astronauts. No government is reported to have acted on any of this.

The project is thought to have ended when he died in 1970, three years after the Outer Space Treaty barred countries from claiming space. Mangan's stated aim was close to the treaty's outcome, in that no country may own space. His only legal step was a county filing, and no government treated it as giving him anything.

add_sources.t: Outer Space Treaty, full text (UN Office for Outer Space Affairs)

chandrayaan-3.story:
Chandrayaan-3 was an Indian Space Research Organisation mission that put the Vikram lander and the small Pragyan rover near the Moon's south pole, at about 69 degrees south, on 23 August 2023. India went there partly because studies show large amounts of ice in the region. It had lost an earlier lander, Chandrayaan-2, in 2019. The rover worked nearby for about 12 days before being put to sleep ahead of the lunar night. Both machines remain at the site.

India calls the site Shiv Shakti point. The International Astronomical Union, the body that names features in space, accepted the name Statio Shiv Shakti in 2024. A name has no legal effect on who may use a place. Article II of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, the main international agreement on space, bars claims to the Moon by any means. Article VIII leaves legal authority over the machines with India as the registering country.

Under Article IX, a later mission from another country must act with due regard for what others are doing there, and nothing in the treaty stops it landing nearby.

change-4.story:
Chang'e 4 was a Chinese robotic mission that made the first soft landing on the far side of the Moon, on 3 January 2019, inside Von Kármán crater in the South Pole-Aitken Basin. The Moon always turns the same face towards Earth, so a craft on the far side cannot talk directly to Earth. China first placed a relay satellite called Queqiao beyond the Moon to pass signals on. The lander and the Yutu-2 rover are both still on the surface.

Article VIII of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, the main international agreement on space, gives legal authority over a spacecraft to the country that registers it, which here means China. Article II bars claims to land on the Moon, so being first on the far side gives China no title to the crater, and a later mission from any country may land nearby.

The relay satellite shows a practical dependence. A far side base needs a line of communication through orbit, and the treaty does not treat holding such a line as a form of ownership.

change-6.story:
Chang'e 6 was a Chinese robotic mission that collected rock and soil from the far side of the Moon. It landed on 1 June 2024 in the southern part of Apollo Basin. It collected 1,935.3 grams of samples. Its ascent stage carried them back into orbit, and the return capsule reached Inner Mongolia on 25 June. The descent stage stayed behind.

Article VIII of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, the main international agreement on space, keeps legal authority over that hardware with China, and ownership continues whether an object stays on the Moon or returns to Earth.

Samples raise a harder question. Taking them created no claim to the site, because Article II bars any country from claiming land on the Moon. The treaty does not plainly say how soil from land no country may own comes to be owned once removed. Whether taking resources is allowed before any international system exists is disputed between the Artemis Accords and the Moon Agreement, and any settlement that means to live off local materials would depend on the answer.

add_sources.t: Artemis Accords (Wikipedia)
The Moon Agreement: hanging by a thread (McGill)
